entries.title: ‘I Was Being Provocative,’ Talarico Says of Past Comment on God’s Gender
entries.summary: The Texas Democrat said he is still learning how to communicate “without muddying the waters.”
entries.content:
A week before early voting begins in Texas, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico attempted to account for past statements that have ended up as attack-ad fodder.

Select voters in the audience at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media repeatedly pressed Talarico on controversial comments dogging his bid to be the first Democrat elected statewide in 32 years.

Sarah Gardner, a voter from Talarico’s hometown of Round Rock, confronted the candidate directly about his comment that “God is nonbinary” and told him that it has “led a lot of Christian voters to question the authenticity” of his faith.

“The first comment about God not being defined by gender, when I said that, I was being provocative,” said Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian who frequently references his religious beliefs in his politics. “I think what I was saying is actually not controversial theologically; the idea that we can't define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that. The late Pope Benedict said that.”

Gardner responded that she believes Talarico should be more careful about using “modern cultural terms when talking about God,” and Talarico welcomed the criticism.

“Preachers often will say something shocking in a sermon to get your attention,” Talarico said. “That's something I'm still learning how to do in a responsible way … where I'm actually communicating what I mean and not muddying the waters.”

CNN anchor and moderator Erin Burnett also questioned Talarico’s 2020 comments on capitalism when he told the Austin Sierra Club that he believes capitalism is an “oppressive system.” In recent months, Talarico’s campaign has described the candidate as a “proud capitalist.”

Talarico responded that the media had taken “one sentence out of a long conversation” and used it “to try to paint a picture” of his stance.

“I was talking about the system we have now, which is actually not capitalism. It's crony capitalism. What’s rewarded in this economy is people who can pay for access,” Talarico said. “What I'm trying to get back to is OG capitalism.”

Pressed by Burnett, Talarico also said that his comment during a Democratic Senate primary debate that it was “time to tear down this secret police force and replace it” wasn’t meant to be seen as an explicit call for the abolition of ICE.

Talarico avoided mentioning his Republican opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, until the event’s final moments, saying that he does not want to convince Texans to vote “against” Paxton but rather for his policies on their own merit. Talarico says Paxton has dodged his repeated calls for a debate, and Burnett said that while Paxton was invited to attend the town hall, CNN had not received a response.

entries.title: Capitals Beat Canadiens, 5-4
entries.summary: Alex Tuch scored twice and added an assist.
entries.content:
By Sammi Silber

Alex Tuch scored twice and added an assist and the Washington Capitals beat the Montreal Canadiens 5-4 on Wednesday night.

Jordan Kyrou had a goal and assist, Justin Holl and Ivan Miroshnichenko also scored and Charlie Lindgren stopped 26 shots to help the Capitals snap a two-game losing streak.

Josh Anderson scored twice and Lane Hutson and Nick Suzuki added goals for the Canadiens.

Both teams played on Tuesday night, with Washington falling 4-2 at Carolina, and Montreal edging Buffalo 4-3 in a shootout at home.

Montreal got off to a quick start when Anderson, alone at the net front, buried a feed from Alex Newhook 4:56 into play. Minutes later, Kryou responded, cutting to the middle before rifling a quick shot past Jakub Dobes.

Roughly halfway through the first, Montreal regained the lead, as Hutson, playing against younger brother Cole for the first time, beat Charlie Lindgren on a quick shot from the slot. With 25 seconds to go in the period, the Capitals tied it 2 on a power play. Ivan Miroshnichenko’s backdoor feed to Tuch went off Anderson’s stick and in.

Washington took a 3-2 lead 6:16 into the second period, when Tuch had a short-handed goal. Anderson tied it again from close range.

Justin Holl broke the tie with 7:31 minutes to go, beating Dobes on a point shot through traffic. Tuch added an insurance goal minutes later for his fifth of the season.

Suzuki pulled the Canadiens within one with 1:39 to go on a power play with an extra attacker.

entries.title: Candidates Are Increasingly Icing Out Reporters on the Campaign Trail
entries.summary: One press freedom advocate said they’ve observed a concerning “normalization of hostility and aggressive pushback to journalists” across the country.
entries.content:
From the White House grounds to town halls across the country, politicians and candidates have been attempting to block members of the media from covering them — and advocates say it’s raising serious press freedom concerns.

The trend has stretched beyond party lines and political positions. Sometimes incidents stem from a dispute over unfavorable coverage; others from logistics snags or credentialing issues. But clashes between politicians and members of the media appear to have reached a fever pitch.

Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland) on Tuesday tried to bar reporter Cat Murphy from recording him after a campaign forum with his Democratic challenger, incorrectly citing the state’s two-party consent law, which does not apply to public press gaggles. The incident, in which Harris called for an officer to take the journalist’s camera before abruptly exiting the room, occurred the same day a federal judge extended a block on President Donald Trump from barring some journalists from the White House grounds.

The Society of Professional Journalists, a national organization that issues standards for ethical reporting and advocates for press freedom and access, said it was “deeply concerned” by the representative’s threat to involve law enforcement while Murphy, a student journalist from the University of Maryland, was attempting to record Harris’ post-debate remarks.

The First Amendment does not guarantee journalists admission to every campaign event — including private, invite-only gatherings and events with limited capacity — but that “doesn't make it acceptable for candidates to exclude reporters because they dislike their coverage,” SPJ’s executive director, Caroline Hendrie, told The Washington Sun, adding that restricting press freedom is a “bipartisan issue.”

“We are seeing a spread and a normalization of hostility and aggressive pushback to journalists asserting their rights to report in the public on the public's behalf,” Hendrie said. “I think it's part of a strategy to delegitimize ethical, independent reporting.”

Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Earlier this month, a staffer for Brandon Herrera, the Republican nominee for Texas’ 23rd Congressional District, tried to remove a Texas Public Radio reporter from a campaign event after the journalist attempted to interview him about controversial remarks he made online. On Sept. 24, a staffer for Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany — who’s running for governor in Wisconsin — blocked two Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporters from entering a veterans roundtable event for Tiffany’s campaign.

Tiffany later accused one of the Journal Sentinel reporters of being a “liberal activist” and running a series of “articles that have been hit jobs” on his campaign

“All we ask is for fair and balanced reporting,” Tiffany said.

Multiple Democratic candidates have also denied media access across primary and general election campaign events.

Several media outlets, including Sacramento TV station KCRA and The New York Times, were blocked from covering a campaign event featuring former Vice President Kamala Harris and Richard Pan, the Democrat running for California’s 6th Congressional District, on Oct. 2. Representatives for Harris and Pan blamed miscommunications in the credentialing process and each other’s teams for excluding the outlets.

Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong — who lost her primary — initially blocked a Fox News reporter from reporting live from her election night watch party on Aug. 11, with the campaign citing capacity limits for the venue. Staffers eventually allowed the Fox journalist to enter without her camera crew’s equipment in tow.

And Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), who also lost in her Democratic Senate primary, ejected a reporter from The Atlantic from a campaign event in February — though Crockett publicly denied the allegations.

“I will say that, you know, there is a specific journalist who is — she has a history of being less than truthful, and frankly, there’s no evidence of anything that she’s talking about,” Crockett said in an interview with CBS News following the alleged incident.

The trend also extends to elected politicians: Press freedom groups recently urged Maryland Gov. Wes Moore to stop scuttling media inquiries from Sinclair-owned news outlets and sending them generic responses amid his defamation quarrel with the broadcast group’s chair — likening it to Trump’s White House media ban. (The Washington Sun has a content-sharing agreement with The Baltimore Sun, which is one of the outlets affected.)

The U.S. Press Freedom Tracker documented more than 275 violations in 2025 — including assaults, arrests, equipment seizures and access denials for journalists. That number is nearly a 30% increase from 2024’s tally, according to the Freedom of the Press Foundation’s annual impact report.

By icing out specific members of the media and justifying the action by citing a reporter’s supposed bias against the candidate, public officials could be redefining “routine news gathering as misconduct,” Hendrie said.

“If you diligently seek comment from people you're reporting about, that's being misconstrued and redefined as harassment on the part of reporters when, in fact, they're trying to fulfill their professional duties,” Hendrie added.

entries.title: Talk to Tom: Why Do You Love Purple Patch So Much?
entries.summary: Plus: Why doesn't Bethesda have a better food scene?
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

What are your thoughts on why Bethesda endures such a mediocre food scene? It’s sandwiched between D.C. and Rockville, which both have terrific food.

The center of Bethesda is pricey, and controlled by a few big developers who favor credit-worthy tenants — chains and polished restaurant groups versus individual chefs with more personal menus. Staffing is a challenge, too, given that cooks and servers may not be able to afford to live nearby, which affects hiring and retention. Further, the affluent customer base seems to favor what’s comfortable, familiar and convenient. Then there’s the pull of D.C. and more diverse options. Discerning residents can just drive a short distance for better choices.

However, I’d be remiss not to flag some places that I admire in Bethesda. They include the Italian-themed Aventino from Mike Friedman, the owner of the popular Red Hen in the District; the French mainstay Mon Ami Gabi, where I recently enjoyed a good trout amandine and warm service; the pan-Asian Raku; and the Salt Line, the attractive local seafood venue on Bethesda Row with same-tasting branches in D.C.’s Navy Yard and Arlington’s Ballston neighborhood.

Another exception to the reader’s thinking was the late Woodmont Grill, which diners appreciated for its live music, generous portions and a lunch that ran to 5 p.m. The restaurant abruptly went dark a year ago this month.

Can you describe how you prepare to visit a new restaurant?

I assume you mean as a food critic. If the establishment has public relations support, I’ll read the press releases and gather any background on the chefs, owners, designers and others, in addition to reviewing the menu online. But I also do some sleuthing of my own. I can’t tell you how many chefs claim they’ve worked for, say, the world-renowned (if controversial) René Redzepi of Noma in Copenhagen or California chef Wolfgang Puck of Spago acclaim, only for me to discover they spent fleeting time in a short stage, or apprenticeship, at those high-profile restaurants.

One thing I try not to do is read fellow reviewers in advance. That might sound surprising, but I never want to be influenced by a competitor or someone else’s thoughts. I also verify the hours the restaurant is open, because more than once, I’ve driven someplace far from home only to discover that, for instance, the place is closed on Tuesdays.

Other than that, I like to approach a new restaurant with open eyes (and tastebuds). Then I aim to order dishes that show off the range of the menu — different cooking techniques and so on.

Why do you love Purple Patch so much?

Launched in 2015, the casual Filipino restaurant in Mount Pleasant is very much to my taste. No one makes better lumpia. But food is only one reason I named Purple Patch my 2023 Restaurant of the Year when I was food critic at The Washington Post. I value the owner’s story just as much as the cooking.

purplepatch_101426_0244 copy.jpg (8020x5346, AR: 1.50)purplepatch_101426_0113 copy.jpg (8072x5382, AR: 1.50)Patrice Cleary is a former Marine, single mom and caretaker to her mother (and cooking teacher), who’s known in the dining room as Lola — “grandmother” in Tagalog. Cleary is also a restaurateur who once told me she held tight to her dream for fear of “letting my people down” as an ambassador of her homeland’s cuisine in the nation’s capital. I admire her work mantra: Be firm, fair and consistent. She also sees needs and fills them. Witness the multiple popular Joia Burger shops she’s introduced in recent years.



Does a work ethic and a sense of mission make the owner’s chicken adobo and vinegar-and-chile-ignited sisig taste better at Purple Patch? I believe so. And Cleary’s bustling dining room backs me up.


How do you pronounce your last name?


Say SEET-suh-ma — and thank you for asking. It’s a Dutch surname from Friesland, in the northern Netherlands.


My wife’s boss is coming to town, and we’d like to take him somewhere special for dinner. He’s a former chef with a pretty discerning palate, and he’s also a pescatarian. We live in Vienna but are happy to go anywhere in NoVA or D.C.

If you want to stay close to home, book a table at the cozy Roberto’s Ristorante Italiano in Vienna, whose veteran chef, Roberto Donna, once presided over the top-tier Galileo in Washington. The sample menu provided online lists multiple fish and seafood options among the starters and main courses. In nearby Fairfax, I’ve been going to the family-run, Greek-themed Nostos for years. Usually, I spring for whole fish, often sweet-flesh branzino, fileted by a server with surgical precision and accompanied by roast potatoes seasoned with lemon and oregano and pleasantly bitter greens.

An ocean of options await in the city. Check out the chic Barbouzard on K Street Northwest for French-Mediterranean fare from the talented Cedric Maupillier, the petite Lutece in Georgetown for some of D.C.’s most artful French cooking or the swank, retro-looking supper club Occidental near the White House, where the goods embrace Dover sole meunière, Chilean sea bass and a sight gag in the form of a crab-filled avocado. (Sorry, no spoilers from me, but you have to try it.)

If you had the option to fly out to any U.S. city for a weekend to get lunch, dinner and breakfast/brunch before flying home, what city would it be and where would you eat?

Just one city, huh? That’s a challenge.

The strategy that first comes to mind, though, is San Francisco, where I worked for four years as a food reporter and restaurant reviewer for The San Francisco Chronicle.

For old time’s sake, the moment I landed, I’d take an Uber from SFO to Tadich Grill. Lunch is my favorite time to eat at the seafood staple by the bay, which opened during the gold rush in 1849 and has been operated by descendants from the Dalmatian Coast of Croatia ever since. The choice seats are the stools at the epic, 80-foot wood bar, where old-school servers in white jackets point out the grill’s classics: crab cakes shaped from Dungeness crab, the oyster-embedded frittata known as Hangtown Fry and definitely a bowl of cioppino that prompts a server to offer you a bib.

Dinner is a no-brainer: Zuni Café, whose wood-burning oven I can smell a block away on Market Street. No matter how many new places have opened since my last visit, I always make time for what I consider to be the most soulful restaurant in the city. Always, I’ll get a first course of house-cured anchovies with celery, Parmigiano-Reggiano and Taggiasca olives — truly one of my last-meal requests. If I’m with company, the roast chicken is a must. Splayed on a bed of dressed mixed greens tossed with currants, pine nuts and torn chunks of oven-crisped Acme bread, the bird is sublime.

Before (reluctantly) flying home the next day, I’d make a beeline for Ferry Plaza Farmers Market, which has more than 100 vendors and a rear plaza that looks over the water. I’d probably slurp some oysters from Hog Island Oyster Company — yep, well before noon — and browse the myriad shops and stalls for edible souvenirs to take home.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Violence, Uninterrupted
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 15, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Violence interrupters, D.C.’s rat population and Nats manager Blake Butera. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 4/10. 60s are better than 90 in mid-October, but it'll be pretty dreary throughout the day, with showers likely. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

Since 2018, the D.C. government has spent tens of millions to hire violence interrupters in neighborhoods with higher rates of gun violence. But according to a study quietly published earlier this year, those programs have had lackluster results.

Actually, a group of researchers who evaluated D.C.’s violence intervention programs found that one of them was associated with a slight increase in firearm homicides in the areas where it operated.

“The outcomes were not good,” said Johns Hopkins professor Daniel Webster, one of the study authors.

The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports that the findings, reflecting data from 2018 through the middle of 2025, were yet another blow for these programs, which have taken hits to both their budgets and reputations in recent years. Biden-era federal funding for these community anti-violence programs has dried up. In 2024, two city officials, including D.C. Council member Trayon White, were charged with bribery related to city violence intervention grants. And some violence interruption providers have come under scrutiny for employee misbehavior or alleged misuse of government funds.

But the findings shouldn’t negate the commitment of violence interrupters who put their own safety on the line to do their jobs, said study author Joseph Richardson.

“I can see the honor and the heroics and integrity in the frontline workers and their commitment to really reducing gun violence in D.C. and working to improve their communities,” he said.

D.C. Deputy Mayor for Public Safety and Justice Lindsey Appiah said the Bowser administration respects the researchers’ work, and noted that they have made significant recent reforms to the programs that the study findings don’t reflect.





DEEP DIVE

D.C. could end up giving $60 million to the operator of a Ward 8 hospital the District paid to build, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports.

Mayor Muriel Bowser has asked the D.C. Council to commit $10 million a year for six years to help sustain the labor and delivery unit at Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center, the 136-bed hospital that cost taxpayers $434 million. The hospital — which opened in April 2025 — is operated by GW Health and UHS.

“The cost of operating a full-service maternal and fetal services is substantial,” Bowser wrote to the council. “Unlike other hospital services, maternal health care has a significantly longer lead time to financial stability.”

Bowser argues that the communities around Cedar Hill need the maternal health services the hospital offers. But lawmakers are worried that they will be committing to putting more taxpayer funds into a hospital that should be operating without them.

“We all want to see Cedar Hill be successful but we have to understand what is the trajectory here that doesn’t require significant additional support from the public,” said At-Large council member Christina Henderson, who chairs the council’s health committee.

The six-year commitment would also lock in Bowser’s successor, expected to be Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George. The mayor’s request will require council approval in an already busy fall for lawmakers.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Lawyers argued over the National Guard’s D.C. deployment at a U.S. Court of Appeals hearing Wednesday. The Trump administration insisted that D.C. is “a creature of federal law,” which gives the president vast authority over troop deployments. D.C.’s Office of the Attorney General, which sued over the deployment last year, once again argued that the president has overstepped his authority.

The Trump administration had appealed a lower court’s ruling that the deployment was illegal. The troops are allowed to stay in the city while the appeals court considers the matter. It’s not clear when the appeals court will make a decision.

Troubled waters: Errors made during the installation of the coating on the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool caused at least 85 failures, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

Showdown: A group of ticket resale platforms sued D.C. on Wednesday to prevent a law capping the sale price of secondhand tickets from going into effect this January, Kendall reports.

“It’s not surprising to see them try for an encore to preserve these enormous profits and the status quo,” said Charles Allen, the council member behind the bill. “I think their time would be better spent preparing for January 1 when music fans will finally catch a break on the outrageous price mark-ups.”

No more Mr. Mice Guy. D.C. Council members on the health committee unanimously passed a bill yesterday that aims to curb the rat population in D.C., a city recently ranked the fifth-rattiest in the nation. The green-lit pilot program will provide Business Improvement Districts and Main Streets grants for “rodent-proof” dumpsters and require the Department of Health to launch a public education campaign on rodent prevention and the risks of rodenticide. The bill will now face votes in front of the full council.

A missing multimillion-dollar Kennedy Center donation is fueling a feud among allies of President Donald Trump. Trump has ordered a White House investigation into allegations that a donation to the Kennedy Center never arrived, Axios reports.

The dispute involves former Kennedy Center president Richard Grenell, financier Michael Mildon and Alina Habba, a former Trump lawyer who is married to Mildon. Habba alleges Grenell persuaded Mildon to include a donation — nearly $6 million — in a $17.6 million business deal in 2025, but Kennedy Center staff could not find a record of the contribution. Grenell has denied the allegations, calling them “absurd.” The dispute comes as the Kennedy Center faces mounting financial troubles and controversy over Trump’s efforts to put his name on the institution.





FROM VIRGINIA

The Washington Post announced it will be closing its Springfield printing facility and lay off 118 workers after the holidays, WUSA9 reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Pump the brakes: Governor Wes Moore announced on X that he’s pausing any increases in tolls for the next year to give families “a little extra breathing room.”





TALK TO TOM


Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

The sample menu provided online lists multiple fish and seafood options among the starters and main courses. Not far from Roberto’s, I’ve been going to the family-run, Greek-themed Nostos for years. (Sorry, no spoilers from me, but you have to try it.)

In the full Q&A: Bethesda’s mediocre food scene, preparing to visit a new restaurant and how to pronounce Tom’s last name. 





SPORTS

Blake Butera (5443x3629, AR: 1.50)
It's been almost a year since the Nationals hired Blake Butera and made him the youngest MLB manager since 1972. How did the first season go? If you ask people around the team and sport, it was a definite success, a step forward for a team that still hasn't finished with a winning record since 2019.

Butera, though, has trouble fully seeing it that way, writes The Sun's Jesse Dougherty. There were a lot of sleepless nights, especially after any of the Nats' record-setting number of blown saves. And after holding it all in for months, one game — a win late in the season — even made Butera open up to his wife at home, lamenting how the losses felt worse than the victories felt good.

“I threw up in my mouth a little bit.” That was former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin describing his reaction to the Commanders’ end-of-game blunder Sunday. His comments were part of a barrage of public blowback directed at Dan Quinn and Jayden Daniels after Sunday’s calamitous tie with the Giants. The Sun’s Alex Schiffer rounded up some of the most scathing takes, including Packers’ star Micah Parsons saying that Daniels “cost my man Dan Quinn his job.”

entries.title: Morning Sun: Talarico’s Provocations
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What “God is nonbinary” meant. Everyone’s turning Senate staffers into election monitors. Super PAC shenanigans in the Bay Area. John Kennedy, super surrogate. Jim Justice, super downer. A bunch of little midterm scoops. And: The left doesn’t want to talk about permitting reform. 





THE LATEST

A question of faith: Worlds collided on CNN last night as the traditional TV town hall (tightly controlled, predictable) tried to join with the YouTube debate format (looser, wilder). At the center was James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, a man who, with just one false move, could blunt his surprisingly consistent momentum.

About an hour into the strange mash-up of television and the Internet, Talarico spent three minutes face-to-face with Sarah Gardner, an involved Republican from the Dallas area, who challenged him on his faith. Comments like “God is nonbinary” (the centerpiece of many a campaign ad) have “led a lot of Christian voters to question the authenticity” of Talarico’s faith, Gardner said.

“When I said that, I was being provocative, and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico said, calling her critiques of the phrasing fair. But he didn’t back down entirely. “I think what I was saying is actually not controversial theologically — the idea that we can’t define God using human categories.”

Gardner said Talarico should be more careful about using “modern cultural terms when talking about God,” and Talarico agreed.

“Preachers often will say something shocking in a sermon to get your attention,” Talarico said. “That’s something I’m still learning how to do in a responsible way.”

More: Trump Blames Biden for High Prices Hours After News of Rising Inflation • Trump Says Officials Who Leak Information to the Press ‘Should Be Shot’ • Candidates Are Increasingly Icing Out Reporters on the Campaign Trail





FROM THE POLLS


The Senate staffers are coming: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Alex Padilla of California announced yesterday that they are sending a little more than 100 trained staffers to key locations to monitor voting in Senate races for the first time, The Washington Sun’s Adora Brown tells us. Padilla mentioned Michigan, Ohio and Georgia as some of the potential spots on a call with reporters. “They’ll be there for at least a couple days after the Election Day,” Padilla said. “If there’s a need for them to stay days or even weeks longer, we’re prepared for that scenario.”

Not to be outdone, Senate Republicans announced yesterday that they’re also training staffers to monitor the polls in battleground states.

FROM A BATTLEGROUND NEAR YOU


Sen. John Kennedy’s star turn: The colorful Republican from Louisiana is in high demand on the stump this cycle, The Sun’s Igor Bobic and Al Weaver report. “It’s like following the baton twirler in the talent show,” Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, said after Kennedy appeared at an event with him.

FROM CALIFORNIA


Pushing the envelope in the race to succeed Pelosi: State Sen. Scott Wiener has forged an unusual arrangement with a federal super PAC: direct coordination. The Sun’s Mark Alfred reports that the PAC and Wiener’s campaign share staff, a fundraising consultant, a pollster and a headquarters. FEC rules have allowed super PAC–campaign coordination when it comes to paid canvassing activities, but federal election law typically does not permit campaign committees and super PACs to coordinate efforts beyond that. The super PAC denied it’s doing anything wrong.

FROM WEST VIRGINIA


Lowered expectations: Republican Sen. Jim Justice was not optimistic about his party’s chances in the upcoming midterms during a trip to a chicken-processing facility in Moorefield.

“From a Republican standpoint, unless something really changes, I don’t think it’s going to be a pretty baby,” Justice told The Sun’s Tyler Spence after the event.

The longtime political leader of a rural, red state offered his blunt assessment on why Republicans seem to be struggling. “We chase like crazy to save the federal government $14 so we can get on a soapbox and act how proud we are,” the senator said, arguing that you can’t cut your way to solutions. “So many folks are getting hurt, and that’s not what we’re supposed to be there for.”

FIRST ON THE SUN: MIDTERM ROUNDUP


House GOP conference chair will campaign with JD Vance in Michigan: Rep. Lisa McClain, a Republican from Michigan’s 9th District, will appear with Vance, Rogers and Rep. Tim Walberg (5th District) today in Monroe. McClain is the latest member of House leadership to hit the trail, and she is expected to deliver a message similar to the one we’ve heard from Speaker Mike Johnson and others. McClain will tell voters, “On one side stands common sense and on the other stands communist crazy,” according to The Sun’s Kadia Goba.

Randi Weingarten hits the road: The American Federation of Teachers president kicks off a 10-state GOTV bus tour today in St. Paul, Minnesota, The Sun has learned. Future stops include Wisconsin, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Florida, Georgia and Ohio.

Caregiver-focused field effort hits fever pitch: The progressive PAC Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy says it’s knocked on the doors of more than 5.3 million voters in the past month or so as part of a $59 million effort to focus voter attention on the high cost of being a caregiver in battleground districts. Public polling from earlier this year found huge numbers of Americans reporting that they act as a caregiver for a relative and that the role has been a financial strain.

A little Trump cash for Maine: The president’s MAGA Inc. super PAC has finally entered the chat in Maine’s Senate race, disclosing a whopping $44,506.23 on a digital media buy from last week. The PAC had long avoided getting involved on behalf of incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who is distancing herself from the president.

FROM THE 2028 WATCH


Mini, maximized: At an event in North Carolina today, Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) will become the latest potential presidential candidate to sit down with Reproductive Freedom for All’s president, Mini Timmaraju. The group was formerly called NARAL, and it stands as one of the strongest advocates for abortion rights. The issue is emerging as a top one for these possible presidents, and Timmaraju is becoming a key voice. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona have all appeared on her podcast. Kamala Harris is set to appear on an episode that will come out on Election Day.

More: Nevada Democrats Are Suddenly 2028 Kingmakers





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

entries.title: Pelosi’s Potential Successor Is Pushing the Limits of Super PAC Coordination
entries.summary: Spending records raise questions about Democrat Scott Wiener’s open coordination with Families for an Affordable San Francisco.
entries.content:
In the race to replace Nancy Pelosi, the congressional campaign of California state Sen. Scott Wiener has forged an unusual arrangement with a federal super PAC: They are directly coordinated with one another.

The Wiener campaign and its coordinated super PAC, Families for an Affordable San Francisco, are pushing their relationship to legal extremes — sharing staff, a fundraising consultant, a pollster and a headquarters, according to a Washington Sun review of spending documents filed with the Federal Election Commission.

The super PAC has also spent money in coordination with the campaign on items seemingly unrelated to canvassing — a legally permissible activity usually involving on-the-ground voter outreach — including payments for a DJ at Wiener’s birthday party earlier this year.

A 2024 Federal Election Commission advisory opinion opened the door to super PAC-campaign coordination when it comes to paid canvassing activities, but federal election law typically does not permit campaign committees and super PACs to coordinate efforts beyond that.

Families for an Affordable San Francisco emerged on Oct. 20, two days before Wiener officially entered the primary for California’s 11th District. The super PAC, which may raise and spend unlimited amounts of money, describes itself as a “coordinated campaign supporting Scott Wiener’s congressional campaign.”

Wiener placed first in the June primary and is facing Connie Chan, a fellow Democrat who sits on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, in November’s election.

Pelosi, who has served in the House since 1987, endorsed Chan over Wiener.

The super PAC’s treasurer is Todd David, whose work with Wiener goes back over a decade. David was Wiener’s political director in the 2016 state senate race.
Scott.Wiener.1 (1830x1191, AR: 1.54)Wiener’s campaign committee pays David for “campaign consulting” while the super PAC pays him for “canvassing consulting.” David’s son Noah is listed as a member of the “campaign team” on the super PAC’s website and receives paychecks from the campaign while using an email address connected to the super PAC.

“We fully comply with Campaign Finance Law,” Families for an Affordable San Francisco spokesperson Sam Singer said in a statement to The Sun. “Any services provided to the Congressional Campaign that go beyond the scope of a Coordinated Canvass are paid for by the Congressional Campaign, an arrangement that fully complies with Campaign Finance Law.”

The Wiener campaign did not respond to a detailed list of questions about its relationship with the super PAC.

In a statement, the Wiener campaign said that while the candidate “supports overturning Citizens United and will fight to do so when he gets to Congress,” he would not put his campaign at a disadvantage in the race against Chan.

“At the end of the day, when the voters look at Scott’s record, they will see a fighter who has beaten powerful corporate interests over and over again to deliver some of San Francisco and California’s most impactful law,” Wiener campaign spokesperson Joe Arellano said in a statement.

The Chan campaign is demanding that Wiener release records related to his campaign’s coordinated activities.
Connie.Chan.California (3000x2001, AR: 1.50)“Scott Wiener found a loophole and drove an entire second campaign through it,” Chan campaign spokesperson Ian Krager said. “Wiener and his super PAC must immediately end any coordination beyond the narrow canvassing exception and publicly release every contract, time sheet and data-sharing record. Until then, he does not have an independent super PAC supporting him. He has a campaign without contribution limits.”

It is often difficult to determine where one Wiener committee begins and the other ends. The super PAC pays for the “Team Wiener” website, which lists 20 staffers under a banner reading “our campaign team.” At least five people are paid by both the campaign committee and the super PAC at the same time. Super PAC-funded emails promote the campaign committee’s merch store, which generates money for Wiener’s campaign.

The super PAC has raised nearly $900,000 through June 30, largely from unions and individuals giving large sums of cash that are too big for Wiener’s own campaign committee to legally accept. The super PAC is only allowed to accept unlimited donations so long as it adheres to campaign finance regulations. It maintains that all its spending and coordination are permissible under the FEC’s 2024 opinion.

The Memo

Since super PACs may raise unlimited amounts of money, federal election law generally does not allow them to coordinate with a congressional candidate in the way that Families for an Affordable San Francisco and Scott Wiener for Congress are.

Campaigns sometimes skirt this rule by employing an indirect method of communication known as “redboxing,” where a campaign publicly posts details about what it wants voters to hear or see, sometimes within an actual red box buried in a corner of its campaign website. Another political group, such as a super PAC, may then take that information and adjust their own messaging to voters accordingly — without violating federal coordination prohibitions.

Wiener’s campaign takes that approach, sharing a 2,085-word missive on its website that details what would-be voters need to “see” and “hear.” Families for an Affordable San Francisco’s website also hosts a welcome video of Wiener himself and shares the campaign’s Mobilize feed live. The Mobilize site hosts invites for over 100 events, each bearing the disclaimer “Paid for by Scott Wiener for Congress.” Some of the events are led by staffers on the super PAC’s payroll.

Families for an Affordable San Francisco shared a memo prepared by Andrew Werbrock, a campaign finance lawyer and a founding partner at law firm Olson Remcho, that details its interpretation of the 2024 FEC opinion: “[T]he FEC has found that certain types of communications do not qualify as ‘public communications’ and, therefore, do not result in coordinated communications, even if they are coordinated with a candidate.”

“Under that analysis, a PAC can conduct a canvass in coordination with a candidate without making a contribution, subject to” certain parameters, the memo said. Canvassing typically consists of paid canvassers or volunteers going door-to-door or working the phones, it said.

One of the parameters is that the super PAC “may not reproduce or redistribute the candidate's own materials. Such activity would qualify as an in-kind contribution to the candidate, subject to the federal contribution limits and source restrictions.”

Olson Remcho has been on both the campaign and super PAC’s payrolls; both paid the firm on April 16 for “legal services,” 10 days after the memo was prepared. It’s one of a number of shared vendors that include a fundraising consultant, Bedford Grove, and another consultant, KMM Strategies.

Federal campaign finance regulators are broadly viewed as toothless, and the restrictions on what campaigns can and cannot get away with have only loosened in recent years. Because of a lack of action by President Donald Trump, and more recently, the U.S. Senate, the FEC has not had enough commissioners to issue penalties, pursue audits or approve civil investigations since May 2025.

“The law on coordination is, you know, almost a joke at this point because of a series of rulings by the FEC and failures to pursue investigations,” said Ellen Weintraub, a Democrat who served as an FEC commissioner from 2002 to 2025, including four stints as chairperson.

“I wouldn't recommend it, but the FEC has not done a particularly effective job of policing this kind of thing,” Weintraub said of campaign-PAC coordination. “I cannot recall seeing very many instances of the super PAC and the candidate actually sharing space; it's not a good look for sure.”

Wiener's Birthday Bash

The pro-Wiener super PAC broadly characterizes its coordinated activities with Wiener’s campaign as “canvassing” even when there is little to no evidence of such.

Take, for instance, “Scott's B-Day Bash & Office Grand Opening.”

The May 15 opening of the Wiener campaign’s headquarters at 2055 Market St. in San Francisco coincided with the week of Wiener’s birthday, and the campaign promised a DJ “to keep the vibes going” and drag performances “to christen the space.” It delivered on both, per photos and videos of the event posted to social media.

In party invitations and jointly posted Instagram updates, neither the super PAC nor Wiener’s campaign mentioned canvassing as part of the party. But when it came time to pay the DJ, the party was described as a canvassing event by the super PAC.

The DJ, Chloe Young, is also a salaried employee of the super PAC. The super PAC paid Young $825 for “DJ services for canvassing office event.” The campaign later paid the super PAC $275 for “campaign event entertainment” — exactly a third of the cost of the DJ.

This 2:1 split is consistent among other expenses jointly incurred by the Wiener campaign and super PAC.

The campaign reimbursed David $255 for “Campaign event security,” while the super PAC reimbursed David $510 for security for a “canvassing event” on the day of the birthday party.

On the June 2 primary, the super PAC spent $1,338.52 at Costco for “food and beverage for canvassing.” The campaign later paid it back $446.17 for “office supplies” — a 2:1 split down to the penny. Rent for a campaign headquarters is also split 2:1.

Conflicting payment descriptions are also present among staffers supporting Wiener.

The super PAC paid Rebecca Kee $3,000 for “canvassing consulting,” but her profile on the Team Wiener site until recently listed her role as “Events, endorsements, and rapid response across the campaign,” according to federal records. Wiener’s campaign paid her $5,250 in “campaign consulting” over the same weeks, and the PAC paid her another $750 for “project management consulting.”

A key parameter of Olson Remcho’s memo is that “The PAC must either recruit, employ, train, and direct the canvassers itself, or retain a vendor to do so.”

Jose Luis Gandara, a super PAC employee and the campaign’s “Policy Lead & LGBTQ Outreach Manager,” has led several GOTV canvasses, according to invites reviewed by The Sun that were labeled “Paid for by Scott Wiener for Congress.”

If super PAC staff were being paid to service campaign events, and the campaign did not reimburse the super PAC at fair market value, then the super PAC would be making an illegal in-kind contribution, per federal regulations.

Families for an Affordable San Francisco has raised nearly $900,000 in support of Wiener’s candidacy through June 30, per FEC records. Most of that money came from two union super PACs, which each gave $250,000 and individuals, including Andrew Chatham, the vice president of engineering at Waymo.

On June 29, the super PAC paid EMC Research $49,600 for "canvassing polling data." In September, the campaign updated a July filing to include a $24,800 debt — half the cost of the poll. No filings show that debt as being paid per the most recent reports; the campaign has reimbursed the super PAC nearly $10,000 to date.

Paying another committee’s bills can effectively be a loan, which would count as an impermissible contribution. Wiener himself has said he opposes the Supreme Court’s 2010 decision in Citizens United v. FEC that opened the door to super PACs and their raising unlimited amounts of money. He has also dinged Chan for accepting super PAC support from a former rival.

Saikat Chakrabarti, a self-funded multimillionaire who placed third in the primary, has urged his supporters to vote for Chan, a fellow progressive, over Wiener, who is viewed as more moderate.

A few super PACs are supporting Chan. They are contributing six figures each to bolster her run, including SF Solidarity PAC, which is funded by Chakrabarti, who also serves as its treasurer.

entries.title: Bowser Asks D.C. Council for $60 Million to Help Struggling Ward 8 Hospital
entries.summary: The money would deepen D.C.’s commitment to a hospital it paid to build.
entries.content:
Mayor Muriel Bowser is asking the D.C. Council to commit $60 million to support the Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center, the 136-bed hospital in Ward 8 that was built with taxpayer funds and handed to a private operator but has faced stumbles since it opened last year.

Bowser made her request for the money — $10 million a year for six years — in a letter last week to D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson and At-Large council member Christina Henderson, who chairs the council’s health committee. She said it would support the hospital’s labor and delivery unit, which has been rapidly losing money since the hospital opened in April 2025.

“The cost of operating a full-service maternal and fetal services is substantial,” Bowser wrote. “Unlike other hospital services, maternal health care has a significantly longer lead time to financial stability.”

According to Bowser’s letter, the unit lost $8.6 million last year and is on track to lose $11.5 million more this year. Breaking even may be years off, she said, largely because of declining birth rates in D.C. and competition from other hospitals.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

From January through July of this year, Cedar Hill recorded 86 newborn admissions, according to data provided by the D.C. Hospital Association. By comparison, Sibley Memorial Hospital had 1,874 admissions over that same time period, and the Washington Hospital Center had 1,518. Cedar Hill represented only 1.6% of all newborn admissions across the city over those months.

The request carries heavy symbolic weight for Bowser, who pledged early in her 12-year run as mayor to complete the hospital. When she cut the ribbon on Cedar Hill last year, she said it would “change the trajectory of health care in our community” — referring to Wards 7 and 8, which for years have suffered from lagging health indicators and lack of good medical services. That’s especially true for maternal health care, as Black women suffer 84% of the city’s maternal deaths.

“Cedar Hill’s opening — the District’s first new full-service hospital in more than 25 years — will play a key role in helping to reduce existing health care disparities,” Bowser wrote to the council last week. “A critical aspect of Cedar Hill’s operations, and an important factor in addressing these disparities, is providing labor and delivery services and building a strong maternal and newborn health system for Wards 7 and 8. Despite citywide gains in reducing infant and maternal mortality rates, they remain unacceptably higher east of the river.”

But Bowser’s request has prompted questions and concerns from many lawmakers, who worry the city will end up pouring more public money into sustaining Cedar Hill even after having paid to build the hospital — which is operated by GW Health and Universal Health Services — to avoid such a scenario.

“We got out of United Medical Center because it was costing us $10 million a year, and we set up Cedar Hill so it would not cost us more money,” said Mendelson, referring to the former hospital in Ward 8 that D.C. ended up having to take over and support financially for years before it was closed last year and replaced by Cedar Hill.

Henderson said she was surprised by how much Bowser was requesting. Initial conversations over the summer hovered around a one-time $10 million payment, but Bowser’s request for that amount for six consecutive years is “a lot more than we thought.”

That’s especially the case, she said, because D.C. already gives GW Health $5 million a year to run the hospital, and Cedar Hill gets a higher Medicaid reimbursement rate than every other hospital except Howard University’s.

Both Mendelson and Henderson said that nobody seemed to have laid the necessary groundwork ahead of Cedar Hill’s opening to ensure it could deliver more babies than it is now.

“How you establish labor and delivery services, especially in a city like ours where you have multiple birthing hospitals, is that you have to establish relationships with the community doctors such that they want to deliver at your hospital,” Henderson said. “If Cedar Hill doesn’t establish those relationships, I’m not surprised you’re having volume issues, and frankly that’s on UHS. All of that should have been done before the hospital opened.”

Cedar Hill isn’t the first D.C. hospital that has faced difficult questions about labor and delivery. Earlier this year, the Washington Hospital Center closed one of its two postpartum units, citing decreasing birth rates and Medicaid reimbursement rates.

A spokesperson for GW Health did not respond to multiple requests for comment. D.C. officials also did not respond to a request from The Washington Sun. But in testimony on a separate issue to the council this week, GW Health CEO Jason Barrett seemed to concede Henderson’s point. “A lesson learned … we should have done a better job of community involvement,” he said.

The hospital reported over the summer that it faced a number of challenges in its first year, including mounting financial losses and long emergency room wait times. It also has faced complaints about the quality of care, staffing challenges and declining community trust.

“I think a six-year commitment locks in the future administration in terms of what happens next. We all want to see Cedar Hill be successful, but we have to understand what is the trajectory here that doesn’t require significant additional support from the public,” Henderson said.

In her letter to lawmakers, Bowser said the financial commitment “will not simply be a blank check.” She said the hospital had already “rightsized its operating costs” and that ongoing reforms “have already begun improving the hospital’s growth and financial stability.” She also said Unity Health Care — a community health provider that operates clinics for low-income patients across the city — had agreed to take over the hospital’s labor and delivery unit, creating a pathway from the clinics in Wards 7 and 8 to the hospital.

But Henderson also has questions about that, especially since Unity has recently undergone rounds of layoffs due to its own financial challenges. On Wednesday, she sent a list of follow-up questions to Bowser’s aides about the proposed $60 million commitment, which the council — including Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George, the likely next mayor — will have to sign off on.

“I know the mayor cannot see this fail on her watch,” Henderson told The Sun. “But her watch is over in January, and I’m concerned about what the future mayor and the rest of us will be left with especially if there are no metrics around how this gets better.”

entries.title: Permitting Reform Is Scrambling the Left
entries.summary: Some of Congress’ most progressive leaders and the country’s legacy environmental groups have remained neutral on a major energy and infrastructure proposal.
entries.content:
It’s been two weeks since a bipartisan team of senators unveiled a proposal to reshape the future of energy and infrastructure projects in America — and some of the biggest environmental groups still haven’t come out with a full-throated position on it.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — the ambitious proposal from Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) and Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico) — pits two core tenets of the environmental movement against one another: the urgency for a clean energy transition and the decades-long fight for stronger federal protections for air, water, animals and nature.

That tension has created a minefield for large environmental groups and their allies on the left.

Major green groups — the League of Conservation Voters, the Sierra Club, the Environmental Defense Fund, the Natural Resources Defense Council — have hedged. They’ve shown modest support for certain provisions, brought up concerns about others and largely strayed away from endorsement or opposition.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), longtime adversaries of the fossil fuel industry and proponents of a “Green New Deal,” have not made any statements about their positions. Ocasio-Cortez’s office said it had nothing to share, while Sanders’s office did not respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

A lobbyist familiar with where environmental organizations stand called the permitting reform bill a “Sophie’s Choice” for the major green groups.

“They’re legitimately struggling,” they said. “Imagine you’re an environmental group, and you have a climate team and an environment side. And the environment side includes environmental justice and clean air and clean water — how do you balance that?”

The past two years have created a unique moment for infrastructure and energy policy. Energy got more expensive. President Donald Trump sharply halted federal investments in clean energy and climate projects. Democrats have “hushed” their climate rhetoric just as a new crop of bipartisan groups, spurred by the “abundance” movement, amplified calls to ease regulations and build big. Meanwhile, the backlash to data center development catalyzed support around local water and land protections and cast blame on AI infrastructure for increasing electricity costs.

These conditions have scrambled political alliances around Congress’ newest permitting reform bill — a sweeping, 400-page document that includes changes to environmental laws that haven’t been touched by Congress in years and provisions that could accelerate the build-out of transmission and clean energy, as well as fossil fuel infrastructure.

“What this bill evidences is a contested fight over different theories of change,” said Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, the executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center, which opposes the bill.

The debate, he said, boils down to whether you believe that the arc of capitalism will bend toward renewable energy.

“Down one path, what this bill reflects is, ‘Let the market rip, let tech, energy and finance capital rip, and then through the magic wand of the market this will lead to decarbonization and robust energy supply,’” he said. “We think that’s problematic because it essentially cedes control over our energy future to capital and takes that power away from the public.”

Environmental groups, including Food and Water Watch, the Center for Biological Diversity and Bill McKibben’s Third Act, are organizing efforts to block the bill over concerns about the loss of environmental protections and benefits to the fossil fuel industry. On Tuesday, a group of 185 organizations sent a letter to House Democratic leadership calling the legislation a backdoor deal and a “massive power grab by Big Tech and the fossil fuel industry.”

On the other side, there’s an unsteady coalition of climate hawks, clean energy groups, AI infrastructure associations and fossil fuel companies who see a new path forward for the kinds of massive projects long stalled by red tape.

Citizens’ Climate Lobby endorsed the bill, saying it would make “remarkable, rapid progress” toward reducing emissions and addressing climate change. The Solar Energy Industries Association said it was “exactly the kind of bipartisan action America needs.” Incompas, an AI infrastructure association, said the bill could “accelerate the energy and infrastructure projects needed to support America’s AI future.” And the American Petroleum Institute called the bill a “generational opportunity.”

Clean energy groups are highlighting the bill’s potential to reduce emissions. Modeling from the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions suggests transmission and interconnection reforms alone could lead to deep reductions in climate-warming pollution, though there isn’t yet a comprehensive report on the net impact of the bill as a whole.

Major environmental groups seem to largely be dealing with these tensions by slow-walking their responses. In several statements, groups say that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is too long to quickly formulate a response.

“This is significant and complex legislation and we will be taking the time to analyze and understand its full impacts,” Sara Chieffo, the senior vice president of government affairs at the League of Conservation Voters, said in a statement.

In a blog post last week, the Sierra Club’s chief program officer, Holly Bender, made the climate case for a version of permitting reform but stopped short of endorsing the bipartisan compromise.

“America’s energy demands are higher than ever and it’s never been more critical that we build as much clean energy as possible, as quickly as possible,” she wrote, adding that supporting clean energy infrastructure is work that “literally saves lives.”

Bender noted some “green flags” in the bill: requirements for regional grid operators to work together on transmission planning; a federal “backstop” that would allow the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve transmission lines if states drag out their processes beyond one year; and protections against power-hungry data centers spiking electric costs.

But her “red flags” — limiting courts’ powers to stop projects, weakening Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act protections, permitting certain provisions that could “lock-in” fossil fuel projects — outnumbered the green ones.

Add to that the Trump administration has targeted precisely the energy projects the Sierra Club wants to see succeed, and the bill as written becomes a hard sell.

Still, the organization’s response is a marked departure from its critique of permitting reform efforts from two years ago, which it dubbed a “dirty deal.”

This time, Bender wrote, “the stakes couldn’t be higher.”

“If Congress fails to get this right, it could mean continued reliance on fossil fuels, higher costs for families, and ever-worsening extreme weather events,” she wrote.

Other major green groups have taken similar middle-of-the-road stances.

The Natural Resources Defense Council called permitting reform a “necessity” but said it was still trying to understand the trade-offs — major changes to the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act that could accelerate fossil fuel development.

Kameran Onley, a managing director at The Nature Conservancy, said in a statement that the organization believes modernizing permitting can hold both: moving faster to build infrastructure and protecting people and nature.

“While we are still analyzing the many details of the bill, we see some promising improvements and hard compromises,” she said, adding that the organization would advocate for community and conservation interests as the legislative process moves forward.

Onley also said the group would advocate for tribal sovereignty in the process. Provisions that would limit the National Historic Preservation Act have emerged as a major issue for tribal preservation leaders. The National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers has opposed the permitting bill, saying it would cut tribes out of the planning process for federal projects.

Valerie Grussing, the executive director for legislative affairs and strategic partnerships at the association, said in a statement that the bill was a “legislative assault on the sovereignty of Tribal Nations” and would be a violation of the federal government’s treaty responsibilities if enacted.

A major critique that has emerged is how the bill was written behind closed doors in negotiations among Senate leaders. The Trump administration’s interference with renewable energy projects threatened to kill the deal several times.

The senators responsible for the deal may be hesitant to accept too many changes. But Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) told The Sun he would work on amendments that are important to tribal preservation offices, as well as “relatively technical” amendments that conservation groups have pushed for.

“But, you know, it’s a planetary emergency,” he said on The Washington Sun Cast. “I’m, generally speaking, hawkish on taking big steps in the direction of clean energy, even if it’s a mixed bag.”

Todd Tucker, the industrial policy and trade director at the Roosevelt Institute, said he anticipates that green groups taking a middle road on the bill will ultimately help the permitting reform deal move forward.

“I think there's a big difference here between opposing and staying neutral,” he said. “I think most of the larger groups are going to stay neutral or somewhat positive. And I think that is likely to give this bill the support that it needs,” he said.

entries.title: Blake Butera, One Year In
entries.summary: The Nationals’ young manager learned a lot in his first year — including the toll of repeated disappointment.
entries.content:
The Nationals won the game. Before going even one sentence further, let’s establish that as a basic, indisputable fact of the matter, that on Sept. 12, across 10 innings at Nationals Park, they scored six runs and the Angels scored five.

Yet when Blake Butera got home, it didn’t feel that way. Or, more specifically, it didn’t feel how he wanted it to or thought it should. In his first year as the Nats’ manager, he’d learned a lot of things. How to tell a player he was being pulled for a pinch hitter. How to cut up his workout shirts to avoid even the faint possibility of bacon collar. He had not, however, learned that when your relievers can’t get outs, there’s only so much a manager can do from the dugout.

So even after his team beat the Angels that Saturday, he stewed. His bullpen had blown another late lead before the offense bailed it out in extras. He went through each of his pitching decisions, especially in the eighth and ninth. The job, Butera says, is to prepare his players as well as possible and then put them in position to succeed. By that description, no matter the final score, he had failed in a few big spots.

It was nothing new, either, losing time and sleep to the noise inside his head. On this night, though, there was a twist: The noise was so loud that Butera opened up to his wife.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Somewhere along the line, Caroline Margolis started reading for about an hour after Butera returned from games, knowing he needed a bit before chatting. But now Blake was talking, venting, wondering why the losses felt so much worse than the wins felt good. And when she thanked him for finally saying all that, he realized how much he’d been holding in.

“I need to do a better job of sharing these things,” Butera, 34, told me a week later. “I’m just the type to internalize.”

By then, the Nats were in St. Louis, the start of their final road trip of the season. They had eight games left in 2026 and no shot at the playoffs, that pipe dream having faded quickly after they off-loaded three of their best players at the trade deadline. They had, though, already laid down a few markers of real progress: more wins than the previous year and almost 10 more wins than the Vegas lines had projected in March. Plus those four months of hanging-by-a-thread contention, charged by one of the best offenses in the sport.

But Butera, the youngest MLB manager since 1972, made fast work of any questions about that. He praised his coaching staff, calling it the best in the league, saying he sometimes had to ask his assistants to shut their laptops and work less. He praised his players, too, noting how well they took to a wave of new data and game day routines. He just wasn’t ready, at least not then, to praise himself. The losing record was one reason. The bullpen was another.

“It’s been really hard. I think the hardest part has been blowing 39 saves. I mean that's real. Like, it's still eating at me,” Butera told me. A few hours later, the Nats would blow their 40th and 41st saves in another extra-innings win. By the end of the season, the count was up to 42, five more than the previous MLB record.

Another lesson of his first season in charge: When your relievers can’t get high-leverage outs, rock bottom is hard to find.

“A lot of times when I talk to the front office, they're basically telling me, like: ‘That was the right move, that's exactly what you should have done, it just hasn't worked out,’” he continued. “And that's why I talk about the process. You know, sometimes your process can be right, the result can be bad. … But at the end of the day, there had to be a way that I could have prevented, you know, even just two of those blown saves. So I'm always looking myself in the mirror, and like that's what's made this year so hard. Just what could have been, you know, having the opportunity to blow 39 saves means that our position players played pretty well.”

He looked out at the field at Busch Stadium and seemed, honestly, pretty damn tired. I asked him, then, about the toll of so much self-examination over six months.

“Yeah, yeah, we’re drained,” he said. “When you blow this many saves and finish with a below .500 record, there are a lot of nights I haven't slept because I’m trying to figure out ways to get us more wins and prevent some of those very hard blown saves. And whether there is something I could have done or not, I'm always going to look at it like it’s on me, like I let them down.”

Who, exactly?

“The team, the coaches, the front office, the organization, the people who hired me. The city of D.C. Heck, everyone who works at Nationals Park, the people selling food, taking tickets.”He looked out at the field again, squinting.

“Yeah, I mean, I owe it to all of them.”

* * *

Paul Toboni could have played it safe last October. Or at the very least, he could have played it a bit safer. He was, after all, in his first month as the Nats’ president of baseball operations. He was also just 35, young for any executive job in the sport, let alone one that would require an immediate overhaul of an entire organization.

Toboni, though, had little interest in the easy, intuitive choices for the team’s next manager. What he wanted to avoid — what he had identified as a potential trap — was making a hire that someone on ESPN praised because he’d landed a top name of the cycle. He wasn’t worried about convention or perception. He was worried about missing an opportunity.

So with that in mind, Toboni sent a quick text to Mike Gambino, the head coach at Penn State: Blake Butera? Knowing Toboni was filling out his major and minor league staffs, Gambino’s response was simple, too: Hire him. No brainer. Gambino, who coached Butera at Boston College, didn’t even ask what Toboni was thinking for him. Butera had already been a minor league manager and was now the Rays’ farm director. Gambino figured any high-up job in player development was the perfect fit.

“And then he called and told me he was considering Blake for major league manager,” Gambino told me. “I’m like: ‘Oh. Oh, wow.’ But that didn’t change my answer, of course. It was still yes, yes, yes.” When Gambino was recruiting Butera out of Louisiana, he had just taken the job at Boston College, where the Eagles were in a rebuild of sorts. Gambino needed baseball junkies to reset the program’s culture. To that end, he needed guys who could stomach a good bit of losing with the goal of winning later. (Sound familiar?)
Blake Butera (5373x3582, AR: 1.50)For Butera, that meant starting as a freshman for a team that finished 22-33, including a 10-20 record in its conference. And if the Eagles were blown out, Gambino noticed Butera taking it particularly hard, blaming himself for the loss over tiny details. Like, for example, maybe BC wouldn’t have lost 9-2 if Butera had known to move 3 feet to his left before a pitch, which resulted in a ground ball that went just past him at second base. It was a kind of mental torture, Gambino thought, but he also knew where Butera was coming from. He felt like he could relate.

At first, Gambino focused on easing the burden on Butera, letting him maintain a high standard without going insane. Later, though, when Butera was a clubhouse veteran, the coach would walk him through the strategic reasons for the occasional blowout loss. If, say, Gambino didn’t think the Eagles could come back in a tight game, he might turn to a young reliever to eat innings, which might make a deficit balloon from 4-2 to 9-2. The score, then, didn’t come about because Butera narrowly missed one ground ball. Sometimes it was a choice, in a sense, and Butera could have done absolutely nothing to change it.

“He liked learning all of that and had a knack for it,” Gambino said. “But it still never made him go any easier on himself.”

* * *

After three years at Boston College, Butera was drafted by the Rays in the 35th round of the 2015 draft, pick No. 1,048. He would, in total, play in 80 minor league games across two summers, never making it higher than low-A. He also hit three home runs, one of which made a Rays team official unofficially rename a tree.

Yes, a tree.

Mitch Lukevics is a baseball lifer, having spent the last two decades in player development with Tampa Bay. On July 20, 2016, he was at H.P. Hunnicutt Field, then the home of the Princeton Rays, when Butera hit a homer that barely cleared the wall in left-center field. A few feet from the fence, there was a tree Lukevics started calling “the Butera Tree,” a loving joke about Butera’s lack of pop.

Once someone makes it far enough in sports, little tidbits from their past morph into metaphors to make a bigger point, to explain what and how and why. And the Butera Tree illustrates a player who got everything he could out of a listed frame of 5-foot-9 and 175 pounds. When, after that 2016 season, the Rays approached him about retiring to start as a minor league coach, the choice was easy. He didn’t fret about losing the identity he had spent decades building. He knew it was time.

“I hear a lot of people talk about how hard it is at first, because they think they could have done just a bit more,” Butera said. “But look at me: I’m short, I’m small. I still got drafted to play professionally in spite of that. At the end of your career, at the end of the night, if you can look in the mirror and say, ‘Yeah, I did everything I could,’ then you’ll be able to live with yourself.”

And so that’s now a metaphor for a manager who knows himself, including what he doesn’t know.

“It’s a self-awareness that not a lot of young men in this game have,” Lukevics said. “So I don’t care how green he maybe was for the managing job. A person who’s willing to admit their mistakes is going to get better, right? It’s not fun, either. No one likes doing that. But I think he always will, because he always has.”

Over three days in late September, I asked as many people as I could what stood out about Butera in his first season. One coach mentioned that Butera always walked with his head up, making eye contact with everyone he passes. Another complimented how Butera juggled all of the team’s pregame, postgame and player-specific meetings — adding that the Nats, an org now run by young millennials, must lead the league in Slack messages. And another coach said that given how well Butera commands a room, he wished he would pick even more spots to address the team and staff. That coach assumed this would come with more time in the job. (The same day he told me this, Butera benched James Wood, his best player, for not hustling to first base and then quickly addressed it in a quiet chat with Wood in front of his teammates and reporters in the clubhouse.)
Blake Butera (5702x3801, AR: 1.50)But in one way or another, everyone I spoke with talked about how Butera solicited feedback on his in-game moves, especially with the bullpen. After many losses this season, he would sit with Toboni, general manager Ani Kilambi and various coaches to break down what went wrong. They would review how they used data, the driver of many strategic decisions, and when they trusted their gut to deviate from the plan. They would also pore over the next roster move, spending six months shuttling in rookies, waiver claims and scrap-heap signings. And night after night, game after game, blown save after blown save, Butera was at the center of those discussions, pushing the room to critique him as much as they saw fit.

“It really upsets him when we lose a game or whatever it might be,” Toboni said. “But one of the big reasons why he is upset, we kind of have a little bit of a funky definition of integrity, which is basically when you feel like there's a chance that you are not doing your job, that really upsets you, because deep down inside it hurts you that you're letting your teammates down. Blake has that to like the nth degree.”

* * *

A few hours after our conversation at Busch Stadium, it was happening again. The Nationals had a three-run lead at the start of the seventh. But then the leadoff batter reached on an error, then scored when Richard Lovelady, a lefty reliever, made a throwing error that turned the inning sideways with one out. With two outs, a single shaved the Nats’ lead by another run. So Butera took a slow walk to the mound, replacing Lovelady with Jack Sinclair. The manager kicked some dirt off the rubber, cleaning it for Sinclair, before handing him the ball and patting his shoulder. And then, back in the dugout, Butera took his seat by the steps and watched. And hoped. And at one point, after Sinclair fell behind in a count, Butera put his hands on his knees and leaned forward, as if he were sick on an airplane.

Yeah, yeah, we’re drained, he had said, and here was what that looked like in practice. Rubbing his palms on his pants. Covering his mouth to mutter something to Simon Mathews, his pitching coach. Another single put two runners on. Butera spit on the ground. But Sinclair wiggled out of the mess, stranding a pair on the base paths.

The Nats would go on to blow another late lead before pulling out a victory, just like in that game against the Angels. And soon, once the season ended, they would start their autopsy of the first year of a new era, including a hard, painful look at how they managed and constructed their pen.

But for now, with disaster averted for a short while longer, I could see Butera’s deep breath from the fourth deck of the stadium. Activity swirled around him, the well-oiled choreography of flipping from defense to offense, the dugout swelling with the nine players who came in from the field. He seemed, in that moment, to take a second or two to himself, a pause before the next decision tied knots inside his brain. And it looked, all at once, like both a hard and easy place to feel alone.
