entries.title: How D.C.’s Investment in Community Anti-Violence Programs Unraveled
entries.summary: The District spent millions on community violence intervention, but according to one study, the programs actually led to an increase in gun violence.
entries.content:
Earlier this year, a group of researchers quietly published a study with a stunning finding: A D.C. government-funded program aimed at reducing gun violence was actually associated with a slight increase in firearm fatalities in certain neighborhoods.

The study, spearheaded by Johns Hopkins professor Daniel Webster and University of Maryland professor Joseph Richardson, examined two D.C. programs that aimed to prevent shootings and offer resources to those most at risk of picking up a gun. The two launched their evaluation in 2023, as the city was experiencing a generational surge in homicides. Now, three years later, killings in D.C. have fallen sharply, in keeping with national trends — but, according to this research, the millions the city had spent on violence intervention programs did not appear to contribute to that reduction.

“I am not surprised that the outcomes were not good,” said Webster, who has studied gun violence prevention strategies for decades and said D.C.’s programs had a “fundamentally flawed” approach.

The findings, reflecting data from 2018 through the middle of 2025, were yet another blow for the city’s violence interruption programs, which have taken hits to both their budgets and reputations in recent years. Biden-era federal funding for these community anti-violence programs has dried up. In 2024, two city officials, including D.C. Council member Trayon White, were charged with bribery related to city violence intervention grants. And some violence interruption providers have come under scrutiny for employee misbehavior or alleged misuse of government funds.

Now, as the final term of Mayor Muriel E. Bowser (D) winds down and Janeese Lewis George, the Democratic nominee for mayor, prepares her public safety strategy, the researchers who spearheaded the study are calling on the D.C. government to overhaul the violence intervention programs. Meanwhile, the violence interruption workers who lost their jobs after a recent round of budget cuts are mulling their own uncertain futures, contemplating how it feels to be discarded after years of grueling, dangerous work on the city’s streets.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

For some, “this is the only job that they've ever known,” said Alicia Jackson, who, until her employer’s grant with the city expired on Sept. 30, managed a team of violence interrupters in Northeast D.C.’s Trinidad neighborhood. “What are they gonna do?”
Muriel Bowser Addressing Crime Trends Now Act (7752x5168, AR: 1.50)Lindsey Appiah, the District’s deputy mayor for public safety and justice, declined to be interviewed about the study results and budget cuts to the violence intervention programs, but said in a statement that much of the study’s core analysis “reflects the program’s earliest years” and does not take into account significant reforms enacted since 2024.

Appiah touted the Bowser administration’s efforts in public safety and noted that homicides were continuing to fall in the District.

“Through a comprehensive, collaborative approach across our public safety and justice ecosystem, including violence interruption, police enforcement, and policy changes to strengthen accountability, we have significantly reduced gun violence in our city,” she said in the statement.

And as for the workers who find themselves unemployed, Appiah encouraged them to contact the city’s new violence prevention grantees about open roles.

“Violence interrupters do some of the hardest and dangerous work in our city, and we are deeply grateful to each of them,” she said. “We understand that this transition is difficult. The work continues.”

***

D.C. launched a pair of violence interruption programs in 2018, focused on diffusing neighborhood conflicts that can lead to shootings. One, housed under D.C.’s Office of the Attorney General, was called “Cure the Streets.” Another was housed under a nascent mayoral agency called the Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement (ONSE).

Some violence interrupters made a difference, brokering truces between crews in some of the city’s most violent neighborhoods and at times overseeing stretches of months without gun violence in areas that were accustomed to regular shootings. But overall, both programs ended up struggling, Webster said.

Cure the Streets adopted a model called Cure Violence, which was designed to address large, hierarchical gangs where leaders direct shooters to target people. The problem, according to Webster, is that violence in D.C. does not operate that way and has instead been increasingly tied to social media beefs, music and other kinds of interpersonal disputes.

As for the ONSE initiative, the agency never articulated a coherent strategy for reducing violence and offered little direction or accountability for the community-based organizations they funded, according to Webster and Richardson.

“I can see the honor and the heroics and integrity in the frontline workers and their commitment to really reducing gun violence in D.C. and working to improve their communities,” said Richardson, but they didn’t have “a full set of tools provided by the city to do so.”

A separate study featuring the perspectives of frontline workers in D.C. is forthcoming, Richardson said.

Staffing at some ONSE sites was also “pathetically low,” Webster added. “You’d have to have superman in there to have good outcomes with that low staffing.”

Appiah, the deputy mayor, said “the Mayor’s commitment to this work is clear,” citing consistent investments in the programs.
DC: Mayor Bowser hold Crime Violence press conference (5436x3624, AR: 1.50)DC: Mayor Bowser hold Crime Violence press conference (3996x2664, AR: 1.50)The mayor and Office of the Attorney General did invest in the programs. The budget for ONSE grew from about $5 million in fiscal year 2019 to $28 million at its height in fiscal year 2022 — including an $18 million bump between 2021 and 2022 alone. The increase in funding was made possible by both the city government and the Biden administration, which boosted federal investments in non-police forms of violence prevention.

“Some of that growth happened quicker than the city planned for,” said David Muhammad, director of the National Institute for Criminal Justice Reform. Muhammad, who has been hired to advise D.C. on violence reduction strategies, said that particularly at ONSE, “there weren’t the appropriate structures, accountability measures, data collection that could have made the work better.” Appiah, on the other hand, said the agency “was building the infrastructure to support that level of investment.”

One D.C. leader sought to evaluate and restructure the programs, Webster said: Linda Harllee Harper, who served as director of ONSE from February 2023 to her death from cancer in May of that year.

Harllee Harper, a rare leader who had the respect of both government bureaucrats and the streetwise violence interrupters, knew the ONSE program was “troubled” and set out to understand why, Webster said. Bowser spoke at her funeral, full of emotion as she told the audience how Linda made her believe in the potential of once-troubled young men to turn their lives around.

After Harllee Harper’s death, homicides and carjackings started dropping in D.C., as they did across the country. Many sought to take credit. The police department increased high visibility patrols in the city’s most violent neighborhoods. Federal prosecutors in charge of tackling D.C. street crime focused their attention on building drug and gun cases against violent neighborhood crews. The Bowser administration touted its approach, which included a package of laws that increased penalties for gun crimes, and giving violence interruption staff clearer directions about what to do after a shooting, Appiah said.

But as the overall news about crime got better, the headlines about D.C.’s violence interruption programs grew more negative. Some violence interruption workers were charged with violent crimes. Then, a corruption scandal: White, a D.C. Council member, was arrested and charged with bribery connected to the violence interruption program, a legal saga that is still ongoing after a mistrial last month. A ONSE deputy director, Dana McDaniel, pleaded guilty to bribery and acknowledged that she had accepted money from the same contractor who had given cash to White.

An investigation by The Washington Post this year also found that Life Deeds, the company run by the contractor at the center of the bribery scandal, had been allowed to spend large sums of government money in ways that top D.C. officials acknowledge was unacceptable.

It was unfair to hold the entire community responsible for the actions of a few, Muhammad said, but the cascade of scandals resulted in community violence intervention programs “getting quite a black eye in D.C.”

***

It’s notoriously difficult to figure out why crime goes up and down, criminologists say. It’s also hard to measure the effectiveness of interventions like violence interrupters; how do you track the shootings that never happen because someone intervened? Among those who have tried to evaluate such programs, the results are mixed, with some bright spots: A study Webster led in Baltimore found that its Safe Streets violence interruption program was associated with a 22% drop in homicides over the course of about 15 years.

In D.C., Webster and Richardson’s evaluation yielded discouraging results. Between 2018 and 2025, the Cure the Streets program had no statistically significant impact on fatal firearm violence, it found. The ONSE program, however, found “evidence consistent with violence-generating program effects” — roughly one additional firearm homicide a year per neighborhood where the program operated.

After an early peek at those findings last year, council member Brooke Pinto, who chairs the public safety committee, said she was “very, very alarmed.” She recommended dissolving ONSE entirely and moving all violence interruption programming over to the attorney general’s office, whose programs were performing less poorly, according to the study.
U.S. Congress Muriel Bowser (4500x3000, AR: 1.50)Pinto reversed course after she could not get buy-in from the attorney general and her council colleagues, and lawmakers opted to consolidate all the programming under ONSE instead. The Ward 2 lawmaker said recently that she has been encouraged that ONSE has been moving its program towards a “group violence reduction strategy” similar to what has been used in neighboring Baltimore.

“It’s … completely unacceptable when people misuse taxpayer dollars or are violent to one another,” she said. “We will not stand for that, and it doesn’t mean that the entire program is not worth investing in, in a responsible way with targeted goals and oversight.”

Jackson also heard about what the researchers found — and she was shocked, she said.

She saw the grateful looks on people’s faces as they handed out meals to the homeless. They held coat drives and back-to-school events for the neighborhood. They put together a Thanksgiving dinner that fed 500 people at the local rec center.

And, she said, they worked directly with dozens of people considered at high risk of committing violent crimes. Each outreach worker had a case load of 15 people who they would help with housing, employment and education. She recalled the story of one young man who, with the help of her team, went back to high school, graduated and landed a steady and lucrative job at FedEx. Another young man got into a job training program with D.C. Central Kitchen, she said. In another case, the team worked with another group of violence interrupters in a different neighborhood to quash a conflict that had led to multiple homicides, stopping further bloodshed.

“We stepped right in to stop those incidents before they became violent,” she said. How could a study tell her they had made no difference?

With a new mayor starting in January, there’s a good chance D.C.’s entire strategy towards violence prevention could change again. In a statement, Lewis George pointed to programs in Baltimore, Chicago and Oakland as potential models.
Trump-DC Takeover-Black Mayors (5810x3873, AR: 1.50)
“D.C. began doing that work earlier, but they are doing it better,” Lewis George said. “As mayor, I will overhaul and rebuild trust in our programs.”

Webster said he thinks the city needs to start small as it rebuilds.

“Put together a really strong program that is not built to fail,” he said. “Show that you can do this in a smaller, defined area. Take the lessons from that and hopefully build on that.”

For now, the city is moving forward by awarding contracts across seven wards of the city. Appiah’s office said grantees will be forced to adhere to the new “group violence reduction strategy,” a model focused intensely on the highest-risk individuals in a community, which offers them intensive support and threatens law enforcement action against those who continue to commit violence.

In Trinidad, the violence interruption office where Jackson worked is closed as of Oct. 1. The city selected a new grantee to cover all of Ward 5, where Trinidad is located, but has not publicly announced the recipient.

“Community members were feeling safer because we were there,” said Jackson. “I’m getting calls every day — ‘When is your office going to open back up?’ And I have to say, well, I don't know.”

After what Jackson described as a remarkable stretch with relatively little violence, the police district that encompasses the Trinidad neighborhood experienced its first homicide of the year on Friday, Oct. 2.

entries.title: Nevada Democrats Are Suddenly 2028 Kingmakers
entries.summary: The state’s new spot on the presidential nominating calendar means potential candidates are flocking there ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
LAS VEGAS — Nevada’s Democrats are feeling popular.

“There's been so many people that come through here, and they have been since the end of the last election,” said Daniele Monroe-Moreno, the chair of Nevada’s Democratic Party who is also running for mayor of Las Vegas. “We're just a pretty popular place.”

At least to her, the national Democrats flying into her state haven’t let on about their 2028 ambitions quite yet.

“I'm like, ‘So tell me. You can just tell me. I won't tell anyone. Are you going to run for president?’” she told The Washington Sun in a phone interview. “And no one's announcing publicly or privately yet, but what they are saying is that they know how important this 2026 election is leading into 2028.”

Nevada will be the second state to vote for a Democratic presidential nominee in 2028, making it a magnet now for Democrats exploring a White House bid. They’ve hit the trail with candidates up and down the state’s 2026 ballot, including several appearances with Aaron Ford, the Nevada attorney general who is running for governor against incumbent Joe Lombardo.

In the coming weeks, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Rahm Emanuel, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and California Rep. Ro Khanna are all expected to swing through the state. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Pete Buttigieg and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin all traveled to Nevada last week. Slotkin’s schedule included events with the Democratic Party and labor leaders. Warnock and Buttigieg joined Ford for events in Las Vegas. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has paid Ford a visit, and Kamala Harris hosted a fundraiser for him in California.

Potential 2028 candidates have collectively donated more than $1 million to boost Ford and other Nevada Democrats, Politico reported.

Other contenders have campaigned alongside candidates further down the ballot, including Monroe-Moreno. Emanuel, Kelly and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker have all appeared with her since last year, according to a 2028 candidate tracker published by The Nevada Independent.

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, Nevada’s senior Democratic senator and chair of the ModSquad PAC, which supports moderate Democrats, has organized trips for Senate colleagues and other contenders. She collaborated with the state party and other organizations to invite Kelly, Slotkin, Warnock, Pritzker, Emanuel and Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego to Nevada in the past year, a spokesperson said. She also spoke with Govs. Wes Moore of Maryland and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania about how Democrats can appeal to working-class voters.

“Nevada is a microcosm of our country. I want candidates in Nevada early and often because I know that if you can win in Nevada, you can win anywhere,” Cortez Masto said in a statement.

The would-be candidates are also meeting with Nevada’s highly influential unions. The Service Employees International Union Local 1107 hosted Warnock for a roundtable discussion last week, and New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker rallied on Monday with members of the Culinary Union.

Culinary Union Secretary-Treasurer Ted Pappageorge said national Democrats have to regain the trust of working-class voters, adding that the Democratic Party needs to outline what it will do on “Day 1” if it takes back the House or Senate.

“If you can win in Nevada as a Democrat, you can win in the rest of the country,” Pappageorge said. “Nevada Democrats have to be pragmatic. They have to pay attention to working-class, kitchen-table issues. You're just not going to win in Nevada without that.”

Nevada’s congressional candidates are also well aware that Democrats with presidential ambitions can learn from their competitive races.

“You know what is on the ballot right now is not just about 2026,” Rep. Susie Lee, who represents Nevada’s competitive 3rd Congressional District, said at a faith rally last week. “It is the road to 2028.”

She glanced down the stage at the one politician not from Nevada.

“It's no surprise that the likes of Sen. Warnock are in town.”

Nevada moved up in the nominating calendar after making the case that it reflects much of the country: working class, ethnically diverse and mostly unaffiliated with either party.

It’s that diversity in a battleground state that locals argue make it worth the time of ambitious politicians, and time better spent than in safely blue areas.

“I would like to see more of the presidential candidates who come to town spend more time in my district, really understanding a lot of these people who don't really associate with one party or the other,” Lee said in an interview with The Sun.

Rep. Steven Horsford, who is running for reelection in Nevada’s 4th Congressional District, also emphasized the 2028 stakes at play in the midterms at the same faith event. He reminded the crowd that the state is not only second in the nation on the Democratic primary calendar, but it is also the first battleground and first Western state that will have a say in the presidential contest.

“The message that I'm sending to anyone and everyone is: If you want to win in 2028, then you got to show up in 2026 to help us carry this state, because the election is close,” he said.

The state’s diverse industries are also attracting presidential hopefuls to the state, said Kevin Carey, a land use analyst for Clark County and the co-chair of the political organizing committee at SEIU Local 1107.

“There's everything from your casino to mining to outdoor activities,” he said.

One piece of advice he has for them? “They have to learn how to pronounce the state,” he said.

“Nuh-VAD-uh.”

entries.title: Sen. John Kennedy Is So Hot Right Now (On the Campaign Trail)
entries.summary: The Louisiana Republican’s popular quips and TikTok videos have helped him garner a following — and GOP candidates hope it translates into votes.
entries.content:
HIGHLAND TOWNSHIP, Mich. — Addressing a group of a dozen or so reporters at his campaign event here last week, Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate in Michigan, joked he might not be the main attraction.

John Kennedy, the Louisiana senator popular on the right for one-liners delivered in a Southern drawl, had just entered the room at a countryside winery and farm north of Detroit. And Rogers quickly gave him the floor.

"It's like following the baton twirler in the talent show,” Rogers said. “You know you're never going to win that thing, so I'm going to turn it over to the baton twirler."

The two-term senator has become one of the most public faces in the upper chamber due in large part to his folksy aphorisms that have been blasted far and wide. He’s become a staple of cable news and social media, where clips of his questioning of individuals before committees frequently go viral.

Only helping matters is his best-selling book “How to Test Negative for Stupid,” which reached No. 1 on The New York Times bestsellers list and remained on it for nearly half a year.
Mike Rogers and Sen. John Kennedy (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)It’s also turned him into a go-to surrogate for battleground Republican Senate candidates in a tough political environment where an appearance by President Donald Trump might not necessarily help. In recent weeks, Kennedy has stumped for candidates in Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Nebraska, Ohio and Alaska.

“John is a celebrity senator beloved by Republicans,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) told The Washington Sun. “He draws praise from people who like his politics and those who like him. He’s easy to like. We need more people to like more Republicans. I’m glad he’s on our side.”

Kennedy is also prodigious on another front: fundraising.

One senior Senate Republican aide told The Sun that Kennedy, alongside Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), is at the top of the conference in raking in online contributions.

“He's been raising a shitload of money online for years,” the aide said. “He's building a bigger presence.”

At his event stumping for Rogers in Michigan last week, Kennedy was greeted with a celebrity-like reception by hundreds of supporters clad in flannel and cowboy hats. Cell phones lit up all over a huge barn as people filmed his speech, which was heavy on Southern expressions and familiar punchlines about liberals.

“You can do what you want, but to me, kale tastes like I'd rather be fat,” he said, eliciting a huge wave of laughter.

Another Kennedy barn burner? “When you pass a ditch here in Michigan, you go, ‘OK, that’s a ditch.’ When we pass a ditch in Louisiana, we see dinner.”

The crowd ate it up, giving him a standing ovation.

But Kennedy also sprinkled in pointed critiques about Washington, where Republicans control the White House and both chambers of Congress. Those digs at his own colleagues have led to speculation about a potential 2028 presidential run, which he said recently he is considering. He conceded that he’s leaning toward running for reelection, but that could change if the party’s crop of candidates are “a bunch of goobers.”
Senator John N Kennedy (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)El-SayedandRogers_RMorton-54 copy.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)“Nobody's coming to save us but ourselves, folks,” Kennedy said in Michigan. “The water in Washington, D.C., is not going to clear up until you get the pigs out of the creek. And you gotta keep the pigs out of the creek.”

Dayne Webb, a college student from Kalamazoo, Michigan, said the 74-year-old senator is popular with young conservatives like himself, including some who are turned off by Trump.

“He's funny and he seems to capture my generation's attention, especially on TikTok,” Webb told The Sun. He said the Louisiana senator’s presence on the platform is boosting his popularity. “When he started talking about maybe running for president, people on TikTok were like, ‘I hate Trump, but I love John Kennedy.’”

Kennedy has made waves during other campaign stops. During one in Nebraska to help Sen. Pete Ricketts’ reelection bid, Kennedy mused that he liked the state “better than sex.”

“Not really,” he said to howls in the crowd. “But I love Nebraska.”

One GOP operative who recently saw Kennedy on the stump in Alaska said that his appearance was a “hoot.”

“In an environment where people are so saturated with nonstop negative ads, it was refreshing to hear from somebody who cut through it all with a little humor and a lot of straight talk,” the operative said.

Strategists are also quick to note that there’s more to Kennedy than just endless aphorisms. He attended Oxford University and is considered one of the sharpest questioners on the Senate Judiciary Committee, where he has tripped up both Democratic and Republican judicial nominees.

“He's an incredibly intelligent and thoughtful person. I think people don't fully grasp that until they pay attention to what he is doing and how he is doing it,” one Louisiana-based Republican operative said.
El-SayedandRogers_RMorton-41 copy.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)“Everyone knows the quips, but people take him seriously on the policy side, beyond the Fox News stuff,” added another Republican operative. In addition to his work on judicial nominations, Kennedy has been active on banking policy.

But Kennedy has also drawn sharp criticism from Democrats, who suspect his accent is an act. A photo of his involvement in the bungled “gotcha” attempt on former special counsel Jack Smith by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri) at a Senate hearing last month went viral. And Rogers’ Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, lashed out at Kennedy last week after he implied El-Sayed is a terrorist who “sleeps in a bin Laden jersey.”

“That’s rich coming from someone who wears his bed sheets out at night,” El-Sayed wrote in a post on X.

El-Sayed also mocked Rogers for campaigning with Kennedy at a barn last week.

“So it'll be Kennedy telling jokes to animals and Mike Rogers sitting there? Should be a lot of fun,” he told reporters at an event in Grand Rapids, Michigan.

But Republicans are glad Kennedy is on the campaign trail to help turn out voters who have soured on some of the Trump administration’s policies, including the Iran war, which has driven up the cost of gas and groceries.

“Kennedy has used a little bit more finesse than me when he disagrees with the president. He's the right sort of person to appeal … beyond the MAGA base,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) told The Sun, adding that while Trump supporters enjoy his style, Kennedy also played a key role in the ouster of Kristi Noem from her post as homeland security secretary.

“He's the right guy to show some independence and really shows some of these candidates that you got to show some independence in the final stretch here, or it's going to be a referendum on Trump,” Tillis said.

entries.title: Trump Administration Formally Invokes Executive Privilege in Kennedy Center Lawsuit
entries.summary: The move comes as Rep. Joyce Beatty seeks more evidence in her legal fight over the Kennedy Center’s planned two-year closure.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has formally invoked presidential communications privilege to withhold documents and block testimony about the president’s involvement in the Kennedy Center’s management, escalating a legal fight over the performing arts institution’s planned two-year closure.

The court filing Wednesday by Deputy White House Counsel Joshua Hoyt asserted the privilege covered communications between Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center staff about the institution’s management and operations.

The declaration specifically identifies requests for documents, written answers and deposition testimony that the administration says could reveal presidential decision-making. It also covers some communications involving Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been involved in discussions related to the Kennedy Center.

The filing comes after Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center’s board, challenged the administration’s earlier objections to producing evidence in the case.

Beatty is seeking information as she fights the board’s decision to close the center’s main building for two years to conduct renovations. She has argued that the discovery is necessary to understand the board’s decision-making and whether it fulfilled its legal obligations.

The administration, in its response last week to Beatty’s motion to compel, urged U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper to reject her request, arguing that she has already received more than enough evidence to challenge the closure.

“The record as it stands” provides enough evidence for the court to uphold the board’s decision and grant summary judgment to the administration, the Wednesday filing said.

The dispute over privilege has surfaced during depositions, including the questioning of Matt Floca, the executive director for the Kennedy Center, who testified on the institution’s behalf on Oct. 7.

During that deposition, Beatty’s attorney questioned Floca about Trump’s public statements tying the planned renovation to the outcome of a separate legal fight over the center’s renaming.

Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 15 that the renovation and reconstruction would not take place if the D.C. Circuit ruled against the board’s approved name change and the decision was not overturned by the Supreme Court.

Asked whether anyone at the center had discussed Trump’s statement with him, Floca’s attorney objected on executive privilege grounds and instructed him not to answer.

Floca had testified that the center takes direction through board resolutions or committee guidance. Asked whether Trump could direct management to delay renovations without board approval, Floca said the center responds to the board and that such an instruction would need to be formalized through a resolution.

“I don’t know what to expect,” Floca said when asked whether the center anticipated Trump might direct or suggest that renovations should not proceed until he received the recognition he sought.

The administration’s declaration seeks to protect communications that could explain how Trump’s public statements intersected with private discussions among his advisers and Kennedy Center staff.

Hoyt argued that the president’s role in appointing the center’s trustees and members of its Advisory Committee on the Arts required him to remain informed about the institution’s management, operations and performance. He said the communications at issue were intended to remain confidential and that disclosure could discourage advisers from providing candid recommendations.

Beatty’s legal team has challenged whether executive privilege can be used so broadly in a dispute concerning the Kennedy Center board’s responsibilities. The administration countered that the president’s official duties extend to statutory responsibilities involving the center and that the privilege can cover communications with advisers outside the White House, including private advisers.

The administration also argued that Beatty has not demonstrated a sufficient need for the protected material. The remaining issue in the case, it said, is whether the board had sufficient basis to vote to temporarily close the center for repairs and renovations — a question that could be answered using the materials presented to the board before its votes.

The filing said Beatty has already received more than 7,500 pages of documents, participated in five depositions and obtained responses to 44 requests for admission.

Cooper previously blocked the board’s initial plan to close the Kennedy Center. Since then, both sides have quickly gathered evidence as the administration asks the judge to lift the preliminary injunction and rule in its favor without a trial.

entries.title: Trump Reverses Hegseth on Livestream Execution
entries.summary: The reversal follows intense backlash to the decision, which was first announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed more than a dozen people during a 2009 mass shooting at Texas’ Fort Hood, will not be livestreamed after all.

The reversal follows intense backlash to the decision, which was first announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday morning.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” the president added.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: Maduro Denies New Round of Charges
entries.summary: The former Venezuelan leader's attempt at a courtroom speech was cut short by a judge.
entries.content:
NEW YORK — Former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro on Thursday formally repudiated the latest round of criminal charges alleging he directed the torture of prisoners, attempting a speech in a Manhattan courtroom that was cut short by a federal judge.

Asked whether he would plead guilty or not guilty, Maduro, speaking in Spanish, stood up and denounced what he called “false accusations and false testimony against me.”

“I reject this document in its entirety,” Maduro continued, until U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted him and said he would interpret the response as “not guilty.”

The former Venezuelan first lady, Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro, who faces similar charges, took a more cordial approach when asked by the court. Asked whether she read the indictment, she responded, “Yes, thank you.”“I am completely innocent. I am not guilty,” she declared.

The couple was indicted again last week when federal prosecutors with the Southern District of New York laid out new accusations that the Maduros oversaw from afar the torture of more than half a dozen Venezuelan dissidents, government officials and even an American tourist who was caught crossing the border years ago. Maduro in court said he had read a Spanish translation of the superseding indictment yesterday.

On Thursday, the judge acknowledged that the new criminal charges make the case more complex and pushed back the trial by two weeks to June 14.

The Maduros, who were taken from their home in Caracas in January by armed commandos during an American military operation, are attempting to dismiss the indictment on the grounds that they are immune from U.S. courts as foreign heads of state. They have described their arrest as an illegal abduction. The operation was part of the Trump administration’s attempts to strengthen its influence in South America and has resulted in an international deal to secure oil rights that have been described by geopolitical experts as an increasingly aggressive policy of foreign resource extraction.

The hearing, which started half an hour late at 11:34 a.m., lasted roughly 30 minutes. Most of it was dominated by silence as the 92-year-old judge quietly leafed through paperwork to decide on a new schedule.

Maduro walked into the courtroom wearing a heavily wrinkled tan prison uniform, waving to the spectators in the public gallery as he said, “Buenas tardes a todos.” He adjusted his turtleshell glasses as he sat down and put on black headphones that broadcast a live translation of the court proceeding. His signature thick, dark mustache was now gray and neatly trimmed.

Two U.S. marshals standing in black jackets flanked Maduro as he sat at the defense table with his lawyers.

During the prolonged silence, Maduro turned to his left to pass a message through several lawyers along to his wife, who smiled and nodded in response. Every time one of his lawyers spoke to him over his shoulder, he covered up the microphone at his table with his left hand.

Maduro’s defense attorney, Barry Pollack, told the judge that the pace of the case is “very aggressive” but “realistic” given the complex nature of the recent indictment — which includes extensive descriptions of the way Maduro allegedly approved the capture and mistreatment of perceived political enemies.

Both sides agreed to return to court for oral arguments on pending motions on the morning of Dec. 17.

entries.title: Inmates Sue D.C. Jail Over Dead Mice, Roaches in Meals
entries.summary: The class action lawsuit alleges the District was aware of “systemic failures” and did not solve them.
entries.content:
A jail in D.C. repeatedly served food with dead mice and insects to incarcerated individuals, according to a lawsuit filed Thursday.

The complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by six people currently or formerly housed at the Central Detention Facility in Southeast D.C., alleges that since July 2023, inmates were served cockroaches in oatmeal, dead mice in salad, milk containers covered in mouse poop and more, all while jail staff dismissed concerns about food safety.

The class action lawsuit seeks financial damages, alleging the jail violated inmates’ rights under the Fifth Amendment, which outlines protections for people in pretrial incarceration. The lawsuit was first reported by The Washington Post.

Pernell Jackson has been in the D.C. jail under pretrial detention since August 2022. The lawsuit recounts that he was served a salad on an evening in late August 2024. Jackson topped the meal with bacon bits, eggs, turkey and dressing, then closed the container and shook it up. He took a few bites, then bit something chewy.

“Jackson looked down at his tray and discovered at least one deceased mouse in his salad. He immediately jumped back from the meal tray and vomited,” the lawsuit says.

He reported the contaminated food to jail staff, who took photos of the salad that are included in the lawsuit. The photos, reviewed by The Washington Sun, appear to show at least two dead mice in the meal. Medical staff evaluated Jackson and diagnosed him with gastroenteritis, or inflammation of the stomach and intestines, according to the lawsuit. He was given pain and antinausea medication before returning to his cell.

The complaint alleges Jackson sustained lasting physical and psychological effects from the incident, including vomiting, loss of appetite, fear of foodborne illness and “fear for [his] living condition.” He has started purchasing commissary food, which is prepackaged and not prepared in the jail kitchen, to avoid the facility's meal service, according to the lawsuit.

He is one of many inmates who have had similar experiences, according to the lawsuit. The instances outlined in the complaint are not isolated and “reflect a pervasive and well-documented pattern of unsanitary food conditions” at D.C. Department of Corrections facilities, the court filing says.
Jail food lawsuit (638x380, AR: 1.68)The D.C. Department of Corrections and the D.C. Office of the Attorney General did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

“The District of Columbia has been on notice of these systemic failures through resident grievances, agency inspections, agency audits, third-party reporting, and legislative scrutiny—yet has failed to implement any meaningful reforms to protect the health and safety of individuals in its custody,” the lawsuit says.

For years, the facility has faced scrutiny for poor conditions including structural decay, inadequate medical care and high rates of death among inmates. A 2025 report from the Office of the D.C. Auditor cites reports of food contaminated with “bugs, rodents, and screws” as well as potentially contaminated water.

entries.title: Election Offices Have Received Letters Containing ‘Suspicious Substances’: Feds
entries.summary: The FBI confirmed the mail was sent to state elections and congressional offices across the country.
entries.content:
The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating after several congressional offices and election officials received letters containing an “unknown substance.”

In an emailed statement, the FBI confirmed a series of suspicious mailings were sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.

“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” according to the bureau. “The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”

The incidents were reported just over two weeks before the midterm elections.

Though the FBI declined to confirm specific incidents, election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma received packages containing an unknown white powdery substance, according to local reports.

Ohio officials said the state had been the target of a similar package that was intercepted by authorities.

The Washington Sun emailed the Senate and House sergeant-at-arms for information.

“Threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy,” said the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors in a joint statement responding to reports.

“Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”

The organizations said they have security measures and contingency plans in place to respond to potential threats and emergencies while carrying out election operations.

The incidents are reminiscent of a 2009 plot in which a Colorado man mailed threatening letters containing white powder to President Barack Obama, members of Congress, and the Argentine Consulate, raising fears of an anthrax attack. In 2023, election offices were also the target of what appeared to be a mail-based attack, with envelopes containing the opioid fentanyl sent to several officials, forcing them to stock up on the overdose-reversal drug naloxone.

entries.title: Ken Paxton Re-Ups His Probe Into Texas Data Centers’ Water Usage
entries.summary: James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent in the senate race, has accused the Texas AG of being cozy with data center developers.
entries.content:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton issued letters to more than 156 data center developments across the state, directing them to provide information about their water usage with the state government.

The request is part of an investigation that Paxton, who is the Republican nominee in the state’s Senate race, launched last month into hundreds of data centers under development.

Paxton said those projects haven’t responded to a water use survey from the Texas Water Development Board.

“Data center developers must follow the law and respect the Texans and communities affected by their operations,” Paxton said in a statement Thursday. “I am actively investigating data centers across Texas to make sure that Texans and our natural resources are protected.”

Backlash over data center developments, based on concerns about water use, pollution, energy prices and AI safety, has grown over the last several months — sending politicians on both sides of the aisle scrambling to address those issues.

Data center politics have also played a prominent role in Paxton’s senate race. Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, has highlighted the Republican’s record of supporting tax breaks for the data center industry and taking donations from companies developing AI infrastructure.

In an ad released Monday, Talarico walks in front of what appears to be a construction site for a data center and says Paxton is “selling off Texas.”

In September, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott halted all permits for data centers until the state’s Electric Reliability Council completed an audit to ensure they don’t compromise the power grid or “put Texans’ natural resources at risk.”

Abbott and Paxton’s efforts to crack down on data center developers is limited by state laws that limit the fines those companies can be charged if they don’t respond to water use surveys to just $500, The Texas Tribune reported Wednesday. Under state law, those companies, however, could be barred from state funding and environmental permits.

Data center operators have defended the low response rate to surveys, with some saying they didn’t receive the survey at all.

entries.title: New Hampshire's Republican Senate Nominee in ’22 Endorses the Democrat in ’26
entries.summary: Don Bolduc crossed party lines to back Democratic nominee Chris Pappas.
entries.content:
Don Bolduc, the 2022 Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, is endorsing a Democratic candidate for Senate this year.

Bolduc was among a group of New Hampshire Republicans and independents who threw their support behind Democrat Chris Pappas, according to a statement from his campaign. Pappas is facing Republican nominee John Sununu, a former senator and the younger brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu.

Bolduc, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement in his 2022 race against Sen. Maggie Hassan, cited Pappas’ record of bipartisanship and support for veterans in his endorsement.

“His ability to navigate the complex landscape of our economy, tackle the national debt with a steady hand, and work towards solutions that bridge divides is especially critical in today’s challenging political climate,” Bolduc said in the statement.

The Cook Political Report rated the New Hampshire race as leaning Democrat, making the seat one of a handful of key races to watch in November as the parties fight for a slim majority in the Senate.

Former Gov. Sununu declined to endorse Bolduc in the 2022 Republican primary and said he was not “serious” enough to beat Hassan. He endorsed Bolduc’s opponent in the primary, Chuck Morse.

Bolduc fired back at the time by calling Gov. Sununu a “communist Chinese sympathizer” who “supports terrorism,” but walked back some of those claims after the primary, which he won. He went on to lose to Hassan in the general election.

Bolduc’s endorsement of Pappas does not reference either Sununu.

Along with Bolduc, Pappas announced endorsements from other Republicans, including former state Sen. Rick Russman, who has backed Democratic candidates in the past, and Sarah Stewart, who was appointed by Gov. Sununu to a state commissioner position in 2018.

entries.title: Trump’s New Press Secretary Addresses Confusion Over Her Legal Background
entries.summary: Katie Zacharia has repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer, though she has reportedly not passed the bar exam.
entries.content:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has finally weighed in on the intense speculation surrounding her legal background since she was appointed to the role by President Donald Trump last week.

In an interview with The New York Times published on Wednesday, Zacharia for the first time addressed questions about her credentials and appeared to admit that she did not pass the bar exam.

Zacharia has for years referred to herself as a lawyer in TV and podcast interviews, but reporting from Popular Information this week found Zacharia was not listed on any bar directories across all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

Speculation over Zacharia’s legal credentials went into overdrive on Tuesday after a reporter asked her where she had passed the bar. Standing outside the White House with Trump alongside a whirring Marine One, she said: “When I moved to China.”

Zacharia told the Times, however, that she simply misheard the question due to the noise from the nearby helicopter, and thought the reporter asked: “Where were you after law school?”

“That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she told the newspaper. “And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president kept me from moving closer to hear the question.”

Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine Law School in 2011, though The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that she failed the California bar exam shortly after.

When she began appearing on cable news, Zacharia told the Times that she consulted with the university’s president about how she should refer to herself. The president warned her not to use the words “attorney” or “esquire,” but said “lawyer” was permissible.

Trump, however, referred to her as an “attorney” in announcing Zacharia’s appointment in a Truth Social post on Oct. 9.

She’d previously served as a senior communications adviser for the online platform and a deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security.

“Katie is a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney,” the president wrote in the announcement.

On LinkedIn, Zacharia also lists a job as “general counsel” at Fix California, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting conservative policies statewide, between January 2024 and March 2025. She also claims to have been an “associate” at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing, China, between August 2011 and June 2013.

On Wednesday, The Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint against Zacharia with the California State Bar, asking the authority to investigate whether she misrepresented herself as a licensed attorney, citing her recent media appearances.

“Each of these representations conveys to an ordinary listener that Ms. Zacharia is a licensed attorney entitled to practice law,” the complaint states.

In California, misrepresenting oneself as an attorney is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in a county jail or a fine of up to $1,000, per the complaint.

“If that reporting is accurate, Ms. Zacharia has repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime,” the watchdog wrote.

entries.title: Flyers Citing Immigration and Voting Laws Appear in Alexandria
entries.summary: Alexandria’s mayor said she was “deeply concerned” by “an apparent attempt to intimidate voters.”
entries.content:
Less than a month before Election Day, residents in Alexandria neighborhoods found flyers, which cited federal laws barring immigrants in the country illegally from voting, stuck to their cars.

The flyers, which residents reported early this week, read “sanctuary city information notice” along the top and listed statutes that restrict voting and residential rights in the United States. The flyers also included a law prohibiting people from helping people enter the country illegally.

The phrase “saving democracy together so no one is above the law” appeared at the bottom, near the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seal and a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement phone number to report violations of voting laws.

A DHS spokesperson told The Washington Sun it was “not involved in the distribution of these flyers.”

Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskins said in a statement to The Sun that she notified the Alexandria Police Department and the city’s federal delegation of the situation.

“I am deeply concerned by a flyer placed on residents’ vehicles in our community in an apparent attempt to intimidate voters,” Gaskins said in the statement. “Voter intimidation is unacceptable and has no place in our democracy. Every eligible voter deserves to exercise their right to vote freely, safely, and without fear.”
HTML EmbedThe Alexandria Police Department said in a statement to The Sun that it is aware of the flyers and has documented the incident for further investigation.

“While our initial review has not identified any criminal violations associated with the incident, the matter has been documented in an informational report and assigned for further investigation in accordance with departmental policy,” the statement said.

Olivia Troye, a former national security official who's running for Congress in Virginia, lives in the city and saw the flyers Monday morning. She told WTOP her doorbell camera recorded someone wearing a mask placing the flyers on cars, and she shared the footage with local authorities.

Photos of the flyers, featuring different designs, were posted on Reddit. One flyer spotted in Del Ray said “Arlington Community Watch,” and another, found in Old Town, said “Volunteer Community Watch.” Neither the city of Alexandria nor Arlington County defines itself as a “sanctuary jurisdiction,” according to their government websites.

In 2017, similar flyers that claimed to be from ICE were found across the District, warning residents it was illegal to offer aid to immigrants who entered the country illegally, The Washington Post reported. Those flyers had “sanctuary city neighborhood public notice” printed across the top.

The Alexandria Electoral Board didn’t respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Texas Democrats Might Finally Get a Debate
entries.summary: Bo French is the only high-profile Texas Republican candidate expected to debate, but he has not publicly said whether he will.
entries.content:
To find a Texas Republican willing to step onto a debate stage this election cycle, you’ll have to go as far down the ballot as the railroad commissioner race.

But even that’s a maybe.

Bo French, the Republican candidate for the agency that regulates Texas’ oil and gas industry who was criticized by members of his party after putting a racist post on social media, is expected to participate in a debate against Democrat Jon Rosenthal on Oct. 22.

Rosenthal’s campaign and the vice president of the DFW Press & Media Club, which is hosting the event, told The Washington Sun the debate is on. But French’s campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The press club has not received written confirmation of French’s participation, and French has not publicly stated the debate is taking place.

Other Republicans higher up the ticket declined invitations to the debate stage, leaving some Democrats skeptical that the French-Rosenthal debate will happen at all. Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party, told The Washington Sun he’d be “shocked” if French showed up to the debate.

He hopes it will happen, though.

“Anytime that Texans learn more about Bo French helps the Democratic Party,” Scudder said. “Texans aren't stupid … they know a scoundrel when they see one.”

French was widely condemned last month over a social media post targeting South Asian students celebrating a comeback win at a University of Texas-Austin football game, saying the “problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

His post prompted Republicans from Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to Sen. John Cornyn to distance themselves. For Democrats, French’s rhetoric proved to be a boon. The weeks following his post represented a fundraising high for Rosenthal, who brought in $488,000 as of Oct. 6, according to The Texas Tribune.

So Democrats see the opportunity to get French on stage as potentially lucrative, particularly as national attention is drawn to the state’s Senate race, which could flip for Democrats for the first time in decades.

One person close to the Rosenthal campaign, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, told The Sun that the Democrat has been going through debate preparation and that the campaign sees the opportunity to take the stage alongside French as a “win-win opportunity.” “If [French] doesn’t go, he’s going to look like a coward,” the person said. “If he goes, I think we’re going to come out looking pretty good.”

JoAnne Asenime, vice president of the DFW Press & Media Club, told The Sun that the organization planned to host several debates but struggled to get Republican buy-in.

“I don't know if it's due to scheduling or other reasons, but the Republican side of things has declined,” Asenime said.

Still, there have been some high-profile election events in Texas. On Wednesday, James Talarico, the Democrat running for Senate, participated in a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media. CNN anchor and moderator Erin Burnett opened the event by stating that Talarico’s Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, had been offered the “opportunity to appear.”

“He has yet to respond, but that invitation still stands,” Burnett said.

Paxton has turned down multiple requests by Talarico to debate despite a campaign spokesperson saying earlier this year that “of course” the Republican would be open to such a forum.

During a recent stint in which Talarico was off the campaign trail, President Donald Trump jumped at the opportunity to point out the Democrat’s absence. On Truth Social, the president posted that Talarico should “immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able.”

Talarico seized the opportunity.

“Ball’s in your court, @KenPaxtonTX,” he said in a tweet.

Another key Paxton ally, Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), joined in the calls for a debate on Thursday. “I certainly think it would be enlightening,” he said during an appearance on Fox News.

Paxton’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Abbott, who has taken part in debates in his previous gubernatorial campaigns, declined debate invitations from Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa. On Thursday, Hinojosa stood on the steps of the Texas governor’s mansion beside an empty lectern and called on Abbott to debate.

Abbott’s campaign did not respond to The Sun’s request for comment.

“I just think Republicans are chickenshit,” Scudder said. “They don't have a record that they can stand behind or defend. So I don't blame them for not getting on a debate stage.”

entries.title: Judge Dismisses John Brennan’s Lawsuit Over Criminal Probes
entries.summary: The former CIA director wanted a court to order the Justice Department to preserve records so he could later challenge any criminal charges.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Thursday threw out former CIA Director John Brennan’s lawsuit demanding that the Justice Department preserve records in its broad investigation into claims that he and other national security officials conspired to undermine President Donald Trump.

U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb ruled that Brennan had raised “deeply concerning” allegations about being politically targeted by the Trump administration, but said he hadn’t shown that the Justice Department was failing to hold onto records that might help his defense against potential criminal charges.

“Instead, he is concerned that Defendants may not be complying with their preservation obligations based on the conduct of certain government officials in other cases,” Cobb wrote.

Brennan, the target of multiple federal probes, sued the Justice Department in July, seeking a court order requiring investigators to keep a broad range of records that he said he may need to defend himself.

His lawsuit says he plans to contest any prosecution that arises from the DOJ’s probes as vindictive and selective and that internal records and communications will be critical in establishing that in court.

The former CIA director alleged that the president — who has repeatedly called for him to be investigated and charged — had singled him out in retaliation for his role in investigating the Trump campaign’s ties to the Russian government in 2016.

Cobb, an appointee of President Joe Biden, signaled that she took that aspect of Brennan’s case seriously, saying that “if he was eventually able to prove those allegations true, that would certainly suggest that his potential prosecution is vindictive.”

At this point, Brennan is not facing enough harm to establish he has a right to bring the lawsuit, the ruling says.

“Even taking all of Brennan’s allegations to be truthful at this stage,” the judge wrote, “the injury he alleges is simply too attenuated from the actions he seeks to enjoin to warrant a finding of standing here.”

Lawyers for Brennan didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The judge’s order grants a motion to dismiss by the government. DOJ lawyers argued that Brennan lacked standing to bring the lawsuit, calling his claims “speculative.” Brennan, they said in court papers, was asking the district court to take the “unprecedented step of managing potential discovery in a hypothetical future criminal case in Florida.”

Brennan contended in the complaint that the Trump administration’s alleged mishandling of records in other unrelated cases created a “very real risk” that he might not be able to access records that could be useful in a future defense.

He cited numerous examples, including the Justice Department’s alleged failure to retain records in its failed prosecution of another Trump adversary, New York Attorney General Letitia James.

Cobb said such allegations were “damnable and unbecoming of any officer of the federal government” but not connected to Brennan’s lawsuit.

“There is no allegation anywhere in the complaint from which the Court can draw the plausible inference that Defendants are actively failing to preserve records that would be relevant to Brennan’s vindictive- or selective-prosecution defenses, to the extent such records exist,” she wrote.

Brennan is among several Obama-era officials targeted by the Justice Department in a “grand conspiracy” investigation widely viewed as an attempt to exact vengeance on Trump’s perceived political enemies.

The effort, run out of south Florida, focuses on whether law enforcement and intelligence officials violated Trump’s civil rights through investigations that started with the Trump-Russia probe in 2016.

Brennan’s possible indictment has been rumored for months.

Last month, one of Brennan’s lawyers disclosed in court papers that a Trump administration official told him there were “multiple ‘viable’ grand jury investigations” underway, including “a ‘far-reaching’ investigation in Fort Pierce that includes ‘issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond.’”

entries.title: Rep. Krishnamoorthi Says a ‘White Supremacist’ Tried to Carry Out a Mass Shooting at His Hindu Temple
entries.summary: The Illinois Democrat said he was worshipping with his family when the incident occurred.
entries.content:
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi was worshipping at his family’s Hindu temple on Sunday when a man who reportedly espoused white supremacist beliefs attempted to carry out a mass shooting, the lawmaker said in a statement on Thursday.

“I'm grateful to those who helped prevent a tragedy, but we must come together to confront the hatred that put so many innocent lives at risk,” the Illinois Democrat said.

“The threat of such violence shows how dangerous anti-Indian hatred and white supremacy have become, and we cannot wait until innocent people are killed to take these threats seriously,” he wrote.

Authorities arrested 19-year-old Alexandros Paporakis of Palatine on Sunday in connection with the incident, charging him with felonies including making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches, Palatine Police Chief William Nord said at a news conference Thursday. A judge ordered Paporakis to be detained on Wednesday, and his next court appearance is set for Oct. 30.

Officials believe Paporakis acted alone.

According to police, the suspect’s car was spotted entering the Aurora temple’s parking lot on Sunday around 12:12 p.m. and then exiting around 12:38 p.m.

Paporakis allegedly told a co-worker his rifle jammed after he went in to carry out the attack, and he shared plans for a second attack, Krishnamoorthi said in a statement, citing police information.

The co-worker then alerted police, and Paporakis was arrested as he returned to Palatine, which is 40 miles north of Aurora.

While searching his residence, officials found a rifle, loaded rifle magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition, body armor and other tactical equipment.

Authorities also recovered an eight-page manifesto. Nord declined to provide additional information about the manifesto, which he said consisted of words and photographs, except to note that nothing in it pointed to why Paporakis considered carrying out a mass shooting. Nord said the suspect’s mother has been questioned as part of the investigation but was not cooperating with police.

entries.title: The Education Department Is Preparing to Offload Its Student Loan Office
entries.summary: The Trump administration is rushing to stand up an independent financial aid office for students. Employees say they’re unprepared.
entries.content:
The Education Department is planning to offload its student loans office, working rapidly to stand up a new independent agency that would take over what has long been a core part of the department’s mandate, according to three sources familiar with the matter and internal documents reviewed by The Washington Sun.

The Trump administration plans to spin off the Federal Student Aid office by Oct. 1, 2027. Richard Lucas, the office’s chief operating officer, is spearheading the change with the White House’s Office of Management and Budget.

If carried out, the plan would reshape how 45 million borrowers repay the $1.6 trillion currently in the Education Department’s portfolio of outstanding debts. It would also raise additional legal complications around the future of the department — an agency President Donald Trump and Secretary Linda McMahon have repeatedly said they want to eliminate entirely.

Current federal law requires FSA to remain within the Education Department. The office is the agency’s largest component.

Inside the Education Department, officials are concerned that the Trump administration is rushing this major overhaul without considering the consequences to families and colleges around the country.

The department’s senior leaders have told staff that student financial aid can be managed more effectively as an independent agency, but current and former officials said the department is taking a chaotic approach that is setting it up for failure. Details of the latest potential offloading remain scant, said one official involved in the planning.

FSA “does not know how to be independent,” that official said, because it currently relies on the Education Department for such a significant portion of its operations.

“They think they’re just going to do it,” the official said. “Their plan is basically just a cartoon.”

The Education Department has taken a variety of steps over the last 20 months to accomplish what McMahon has labeled its “final mission,” including laying off or pushing out half of its workforce, curbing grant spending and signing more than a dozen agreements with other federal agencies to transfer out key responsibilities. It signed one of those agreements earlier this year for the Treasury Department to absorb the servicing of delinquent student loan debt, though those changes are still underway. FSA has 800 employees after shedding 43% of staff since Trump took office.

Melanie Storey, a former FSA director of policy implementation and oversight who now leads the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, said the plan struck her as unrealistic.

“October of 2027, I mean come on,” Storey said. “This is extraordinarily complex work.”

The Federal Student Aid office, established in 1965, was made into the government’s first “performance-based organization” in a law passed under former President Bill Clinton. The law was designed to give the office more flexibility in hiring, procurement and some other operations, but it firmly established FSA as an office “subject to the direction of the [Education] secretary.” The department, not FSA, is responsible for all policy and regulatory decision-making relating to student financial assistance.

The Education Department has acknowledged internally that separating FSA into an independent agency would require an act of Congress, though the department officials and congressional staff said it has yet to engage Capitol Hill. It has also yet to discuss the matter with the Treasury Department, despite its critical role in paying out the loans.

Ellen Keast, an Education Department spokesperson, said this story was “fake news” but declined to specify what was incorrect.

The department “is engaged in an effort to restore FSA as a performance-based organization — not a political tool,” Keast said in a statement. “The Biden Administration weaponized FSA to punish colleges and universities it simply did not like — whether that be based on their tax-status or religious affiliation — and implement illegal loan forgiveness schemes.”

The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment. OMB called The Sun’s reporting “inaccurate” but did not elaborate or offer further comment.

The rushed process has made some inside the agency question whether they are still helping to fulfill its mission.

“There’s a difference between doing your job and colluding with someone to destroy your own agency,” the current official said.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin), the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee panel that oversees the Education Department, said the push at FSA is just Trump’s latest effort to shut down the department without concern for "how much it hurts students, families and public schools."

“I am all for working to make higher education more affordable, ensure folks are not saddled with debt for their whole life, and fix our deeply broken system for paying for higher education — but that is just not what the Trump administration is trying to do here,” Baldwin said. “This is just another illegal move by the administration in pursuit of destroying the Department of Education because they thought it sounded good on a bumper sticker.”

FSA is responsible for allocating $120 billion in loans and grants per year, though the Education Department — rather than FSA itself — facilitates the actual transfer of funds from Treasury to borrowers.

Education officials are contemplating how an independent FSA can set up its own budget shop, conduct its own audits and investigations of colleges and universities and run its own back-end offices such as human resources and procurement — all functions currently handled at the departmental level. The department is scheduled to present its plan to OMB next week.

Lucas, the FSA COO, told staff about the upcoming change in late September and declined to take questions, according to one person briefed on the matter.

On Sept. 30, the Education Department awarded a two-year contract to Accenture worth up to $337 million to provide digital services for FSA borrowers. An agency official said the department is rushing to get contracts out the door while it still has departmental support to enable FSA to transition to an independent entity more smoothly.

Watchdogs and researchers have for years suggested improvements to the administration of federal student aid, but those recommendations have encouraged more departmental oversight of the program, not less.

Ben Miller, who served in senior Education Department roles in both the Obama and Biden administrations, and Jason Delisle, a former Capitol Hill staffer who now serves as senior advisor for the department under McMahon, said in a 2019 report that Congress and the department needed to set clearer goals for FSA and to hold it accountable for its performance.

Policymakers must “acknowledge the importance of encouraging close, productive interpersonal dynamics between senior officials at the Education Department and FSA staff,” they said, adding it “must start acknowledging the importance of FSA through more meaningful and active management.”

Storey said she was concerned the department was rushing in pursuit of an arbitrary timeline.

“The risk here is we don’t do it carefully and we break the reliability and feasibility needed to serve those communities and those families,” she said. “Is reform something we can consider? Sure, but let’s not try to put an artificial deadline on it and drive it through.”

entries.title: DOJ Hits California With New Lawsuit Following Voter List Ultimatum
entries.summary: Election officials in California have resisted the federal government’s push to exert control over the state’s vote-by-mail process.
entries.content:
The Justice Department sued the state of California on Thursday over allegations that election officials sent mail-in ballots to noncitizen voters.

The DOJ is asking the court to issue a permanent preliminary injunction that blocks the state from counting the votes of over 20,000 people who Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services have identified as potential noncitizen voters. In July, the Department of Homeland Security told state officials that the state’s voter rolls included as many as 190,832 noncitizens.

“By sending ballots to likely noncitizens despite the Federal Government notifying California of serious concerns, Defendants (collectively, California) have made it nearly impossible for the United States to investigate and enforce federal law,” the DOJ argued.

The lawsuit comes after California election officials were given 48 hours to comply with a letter from Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter. That letter came with a password-protected thumb drive that listed 20,000 people the department “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot.”

The password, said California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, was on a sticky note attached to the thumb drive.

California election officials were then instructed to hold on to the ballots of people listed or set aside completed ballots received by people on the thumb drive until their citizenship could be verified. The DOJ threatened on Tuesday that if California did not comply, the government “will have no choice but to seek emergency relief.”

But election officials in California have resisted the federal government’s push to exert control over the state’s vote-by-mail process.

“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching,” Dean Logan, who leads the Los Angeles County clerk’s office and received one of Tuesday’s letters from the DOJ, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Weber said she sees the move as a tactic for the DOJ to “cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections.”

“California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls,” she said in a news release on Wednesday.
