entries.title: What It Means for RFK Jr.’s Vaccine Panel to Be MIA During a Measles Outbreak
entries.summary: The federal vaccine committee has not met all year. States are filling in the gaps.
entries.content:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s reshaping of the expert committee that advises on vaccines is complicating state efforts to stop measles outbreaks around the country.

In the face of the worst measles outbreak in the United States in 35 years, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the federal group that makes vaccine recommendations, has not met in over 10 months.

Last year, Kennedy fired all its members and installed a new panel, including several with vaccine-skeptical views. The new committee’s attempt to reduce the recommended childhood vaccine requirements from 17 to 11 spurred lawsuits. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s website says ACIP’s meetings have been cancelled "due to ongoing litigation.”

Historically, the committee has met three times a year. During the COVID-19 pandemic, it met three times a week to review vaccine safety data and issue dosage recommendations. In the absence of guidance now, states have had to fill in the gaps themselves.

In New York, where Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency earlier this month over a measles outbreak, the state health department is relying on new legislation setting school vaccine standards as “an alternative to the standards set by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices,” the agency told The Washington Sun.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order last year that said in light of ACIP’s actions, the state would follow advice from national medical associations, which the state’s Department of Health called “trusted medical experts” in a statement to The Sun.

And South Carolina, which saw a surge of nearly 1,000 measles cases earlier this year, is also relying on outside medical groups for guidance. Dr. Melissa Nolan, a professor of epidemiology who advises the state’s public health department, said “for the first time in our lifetime, the medical scientific community has published their own vaccine guidelines which are different than the federal guidelines.”

The outbreak coincided with an increase in delayed childhood vaccines in the state, Nolan said.

“The state responded in a traditional manner,” Nolan said. “They sent trucks to do mobile vaccine units. But if you don’t engage and address underlying sentiments and have preexisting, built trust with the community, people aren’t going to show up and get vaccinated.”

ACIP’s former executive secretary Melinda Wharton, who resigned in 2025, said that “if ACIP were meeting, there likely would be some discussion about needing stronger language in terms of an actual public health response.”

ACIP would normally review evidence collected by states and the CDC to determine how to alter vaccine guidance and stop an infectious disease outbreak. Public health officials were able to address the most recent severe measles outbreak in 1991 in part because of ACIP’s recommendation for two shots of the measles vaccine instead of the previously recommended single dose.

Outside experts have stressed the need for a stronger federal response, particularly from ACIP. Dr. Paul Offit, the director of the vaccine education center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and a vocal critic of Kennedy’s, says, “It’s gotten harder to treat these outbreaks. We don’t have an ACIP or a CDC that anyone trusts, including myself.”

Typically with this kind of outbreak, Kennedy and the head of the CDC would “be giving briefings in front of the CDC every day,” Offit said.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Health Department spokesperson Grace Jamison touted the administration’s efforts to address the measles outbreak.

Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have “mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country” and “continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles,” Jamison said.

The CDC announced on Tuesday that it would send support to Pennsylvania to investigate its growing outbreak. Earlier this month, the administration unlocked an additional $100 million in funds to help states handle immunization support and surveillance. Jamison said Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin “worked alongside federal teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control.”

Kennedy has long caveated his support of the measles vaccine. He told CNN on Aug. 2 that he has “never questioned the efficacy of the MMR [measles, mumps and rubella] vaccine,” and that he does not take responsibility for the current measles outbreak. He also told Fox News in 2025 that “if people don’t want it, they shouldn’t be — the government shouldn’t force them to do it.”

Now, measles infections countrywide have surpassed 4,000 cases. Pennsylvania has reported more than 1,200 cases. Two other states have reported more than 500 cases this year.

Measles is a highly contagious virus that hospitalizes about one in five unvaccinated people who become infected in the U.S. Measles had been considered eliminated in the U.S. since 2000. However, vaccination rates among kindergarten-age children have dropped nearly 3 percentage points since 2020, signaling that the disease could become endemic.

“It just feels like agency leadership is not really advocating for the agency, not really supporting good public health decision-making, and it breaks my heart for my former agency as well as for the country,” Wharton said.

entries.title: Cities Ask the Supreme Court to Revive a Biden-Era Immigration Rule
entries.summary: The cities in Maryland, Ohio and Connecticut say the Justice Department and Texas used a court to flout the typical rulemaking process.
entries.content:
Three cities and a legal group asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to revive a Biden-era immigration rule, arguing the Justice Department and Texas colluded to eliminate it.

At issue is a 2024 rule that allowed immigration judges, who are Justice Department employees, to close deportation proceedings against people in the process of gaining lawful status.

In an application, the cities — Baltimore; Columbus, Ohio; and New Haven, Connecticut — and California-based nonprofit Centro Legal de la Raza contend the Justice Department unlawfully got rid of the regulation instead of going through the established rulemaking process.

A federal judge in Texas entered a judgment in June that halted the rule nationwide on the same day the state challenged the rule in court. Hours after Texas filed the suit, the state and Justice Department asked the court to declare the rule unlawful and bar the department from enacting similar policies in the future.

“The government did not merely leverage a convenient loss to undo agency action, but rather, announced in advance that it would not defend a disfavored regulation and then colluded with the challenger from the moment that suit was filed,” the application says.

“The result is that a significant regulation that established certain important procedures in immigration courts was erased over the course of a single day, without meaningful judicial review, public participation, or adherence to the [Administrative Procedure Act’s] rulemaking requirements,” the application says.

The cities want the Supreme Court to stop the judgment while the legal case plays out. The rule was meant to spare victims of crimes or neglected children from having to defend themselves in immigration courts while undergoing a process to gain immigration relief from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the application states.

Some removals are permanent, such as a child qualifying for special immigrant juvenile status who is removed before a visa becomes available, the application says.

“If the judgment remains in force while Applicants’ appeal proceeds, it will stand as a working template for any administration that wishes to repeal a regulation without notice and comment,” the application says.

The Justice Department denied the claim of collusion in a September court filing.

“The Department cannot be required to defend a rule it believes is unlawful, and it must follow any orders courts entered against it,” a filing to the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals says.

Texas’ lawsuit came two months after Sirce Owen, the acting director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review, issued a memo announcing the office would not defend the rule in court.

“EOIR’s use of administrative closure, particularly between 2011 and 2017 and between 2021 and 2025, was an unmitigated disaster from a policy standpoint and strongly appears to have also been unlawful,” Owen wrote.

The cities sought to intervene in the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, but a judge found they lacked the legal right to do so. The 5th Circuit declined last month to block the judgement throwing out the rule.

entries.title: Matt Gaetz Faces New Lawsuit Over Alleged Sex Trafficking Scheme
entries.summary: Gaetz, who left politics amid mounting pressure over his alleged sexual misconduct, said he welcomed the lawsuit as a chance to “confront” his accusers.
entries.content:
Matt Gaetz is facing a federal civil lawsuit accusing him and two others of being involved with a sex trafficking scheme, the latest scandal plaguing the former Republican congressman and short-lived attorney general nominee.

Two women sued Gaetz and his associates — now-convicted ex-Seminole County tax collector Joel Greenberg and former Republican state Rep. Christopher Dorworth — in the Middle District of Florida this week, alleging that Gaetz and his associates had supplied the women, who were 20 and 22 at the time, with drugs to help orchestrate sexual encounters and also moved victims across state lines.

“Every part of this venture ran on an exploitative power imbalance,” Spencer Kuvin and Joel Leppard, attorneys for the plaintiffs, wrote in the suit — adding that the men allegedly exploited “financially vulnerable women in their early twenties.”

“The venture assumed that women with so little would never be believed over men with so much,” the complaint states.

The lawsuit was first reported by investigative reporter Julie K. Brown of the Miami Herald on Thursday.

Gaetz said he welcomed the lawsuit as a chance to confront his accusers face to face.

“I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” Gaetz said in a statement to the Herald. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.”

President Donald Trump nominated Gaetz for U.S. attorney general in November 2024, but the embattled former congressman withdrew his name from consideration weeks later after facing mounting pressure from his Republican colleagues and a formal congressional ethics investigation. Gaetz initially faced a years-long Justice Department investigation concerning the sexual misconduct allegations, though prosecutors ultimately did not charge Gaetz with any wrongdoing.

The House Ethics Committee released a bombshell report in December 2024 presenting evidence that the Florida Republican paid tens of thousands of dollars to women in exchange for sexual activity — including an encounter with a 17-year-old in 2017 — and allegedly used illegal drugs, among other ethics violations.

The 17-year-old victim is not involved in Monday’s lawsuit, but one of the plaintiffs contends that she witnessed Gaetz with a girl who was 17, according to the complaint.

The lawsuit alleges that Gaetz, Greenberg and Dorworth supplied the women with drugs in order to facilitate sexual encounters, citing incidents that occurred between 2017 and 2019. The women in their suit also accused the three men of arranging and funding travel for alleged victims of a sex trafficking scheme to Miami, Las Vegas, the Florida Keys and New York City. They also alleged that prominent political figures were also present on the trips.

The young women, identified as Jane Does 1 and 2, met Gaetz in the summer of 2017 after Greenberg recruited them through the website SeekingArangement.com — a platform known for connecting older, wealthier men with younger women.

Seeking.com, which rebranded from SeekingArrangement.com in 2019 to move away from its “sugar-daddy” image, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In the complaint, Jane Doe 1 reported being given $6,000 and Jane Doe 2 received more than $4,000 from Gaetz. Payment descriptions included text reading “Being my friend,” and “car deductible” and “Love you.”

After leaving Congress, Gaetz started hosting a political talk show titled “The Matt Gaetz Show” on One America News Network. Gaetz also serves on the Triumph Gulf Coast Board, which is tasked with distributing money from a BP settlement struck following the 2010 oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

OAN and Triumph Gulf Coast also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
